46	
47	A map directory is normally opened via the map-select UI as the
48	top-level graph being edited. **This issue adds a second way to
49	open a map:** through the file browser, as an *encapsulated box*

59	Encapsulation is a function-like abstraction over a sub-graph.
60	The parent doesn't see the sub-map's internals; it sees one box

# 319 — Built-in library for map self-construction

## Status
open — planning stub. Several design questions need user resolution
before implementation can begin. See **Open design questions**
below.

## Concept

A map should be able to build more of itself while running.
Two built-in primitives, exposed by the runtime to every language
spec, are enough to bootstrap that capability:

- **`create_box(filepath, function_name) -> box_handle`**
  Spawn a new box on the currently-running map. The first argument
  is the file holding the function the box will run; the second is
  the name of that function inside the file. The runtime does any
  build-pipeline work that's needed (compile the source, register
  the spec, allocate the box's input port slots) before returning
  a handle the caller can use to wire the box up.

- **`connect(from_box, to_box_a, to_box_b, ...) -> bool`**
  Attach a wire from the single output of `from_box` to each of
  the destination boxes. Variadic on the destinations, since fan-out
  from a single producer is the common pattern. Returns true if
  every connection succeeded, false otherwise.

Together these let a running map grow new sub-graphs in response
to runtime conditions: a planner box decides what sub-pipeline to
build, calls `create_box` for each node, calls `connect` to wire
them, and the dispatch layer picks up the new region on the next
push.

## Why this shape works (and the parts that need to be checked)

**Single-output-per-box is already the law.** Issue 218 collapsed
boxes to one output. Variadic destinations on `connect` is just
fan-out across that single output — no new concept on the wire
side. The variadic part of the API matches the data model.

**`filepath + function_name` matches box JSON.** That's already how
language specs locate the code a box runs. The API takes the same
two strings the box JSON would hold.

**Handle-as-return mirrors `data` boxes' encapsulation contract
(issue 248).** Encapsulated maps already expose typed handles
to externally-supplied inputs. A `create_box` handle is the same
kind of thing — a reference the caller uses to identify the box
in follow-up calls.

# 315 — Reference-counted compiled-map artifacts

## Status
open

## Current behavior

`scripts/soramech-compile.sh` from issue 309 is destructive at the
top:

```bash
rm -rf "$COMPILED"
mkdir -p "$COMPILED" "$COMPILED/boxes" "$COMPILED/src" ...
```

Whatever lived in `<map>/compiled/` before the rebuild is gone. If
another process — a long-running runner, a different shell, a
sibling tool that opened the artifact yesterday — had pinned to
that exact compiled layout (a particular `pool-runner` binary, a
particular `spec.so` ABI, a particular set of pre-compiled C
boxes), the rebuild yanks the rug. The holder either crashes,
silently retains stale `dlopen` handles, or starts reading new
files mid-flight.

This is fine in single-user development. It stops being fine the
moment a SoraMech artifact is the kind of thing other programs
hold onto across time.

## Intended behavior

A compiled artifact carries its own reference count. Other
programs that depend on a particular build of a map are expected
to *acquire* a reference on startup and *release* it on shutdown.
When `soramech-compile` is asked to rebuild a map that has any
live references, it does NOT clobber the existing directory.
Instead it builds a sibling directory next door, leaving the
referenced one untouched until its holders are done with it.

The reference count is **expected to be unreliable**. A crashing
holder doesn't get the chance to release; an SSH session that
drops doesn't either. The design accepts that staleness is the
common case, not the exception — every reference entry carries
enough metadata to be independently validated and (eventually)
reaped. The reference count is a hint and a courtesy, not a
guarantee.

This is conceptually a copy-on-write filesystem for compiled
artifacts: writes (rebuilds) fork the universe when readers
exist; readers can keep reading the version they pinned to;
generations get garbage-collected when nothing observable still
```

Here's where we left off on the encapsulated-map-as-box issue, and what I think the next move is.

**Input side is done and on disk.** The most recent commit shipped load-time inlining: when the graph loader sees a sub-map referenced as a box, it slurps the sub-map's boxes into the parent's arena with prefixed ids, then rewrites every parent wire that targeted the encapsulating box so it goes *through* the matching externally-supplied data box and lands on whatever the data box was feeding inside the sub-map. There's an end-to-end fixture under `tests/maps/248-encap-input-only/` that proves bytes from the parent reach a write box inside the sub-map.

**Three things are still deferred** — listed in the issue's status header and now on the todo list:

1. **Output-side encapsulation.** Wires the user drew *from* the encapsulating box's output ports don't fire yet. The symmetric splice — every externally-consumed write box inside the sub-map surfaces as its own distinct output port on the parent's view of the encap box — is the natural next slice, since it mirrors the machinery the input side already proves out.
2. **Editor UI.** The inspector toggle (externally-supplied on data boxes, externally-consumed on write boxes) and the file-browser "Encapsulate" action that drops a `kind: "map"` box onto the parent at cursor position.
3. **Recursion** across nested encapsulations + cycle detection at load time.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The decision to inline at *load time* rather than compile time (path A in the issue) or with a true nested dispatch loop (path B) is a third path — splicing happens after the parent's JSON is read but before topology is resolved, so the runtime never sees `kind: "map"`. It gets path-A's flat-graph simplicity without depending on issue 309's compile pipeline being in shape.
- The reason encapsulated maps are the *one* documented exception to issue 218's "single output per box" rule is that each externally-consumed write box is genuinely an independent value with its own semantics — bundling them into a packed blob would have been file-write machinery doing wire-emit work, the wrong shape. Keeping the multi-output exception on this one kind preserves both invariants.
- Reference-counted artifacts (issue 315) and self-construction (319) are blockers for a real release because together they're what lets *other programs* hold onto a SoraMech artifact across time and let a running map mutate itself — until those land, SoraMech is single-user, single-shot.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

1	# 243 — Multi-band comparator routing
2	
3	## Status
4	open · design carried forward from issue 233
5	
6	## Current behavior
7	
8	Issue 233 ships the comparator routing kind with a single
9	threshold and three fixed branches (`lt` / `eq` / `gt`). The
10	generalisation — N thresholds defining N+1 numeric bands — is
11	the natural next step but ships separately so the schema-and-
12	inspector work it carries doesn't bloat 233.
13	
14	## Intended behavior
15	
16	A comparator with a list of thresholds defines N+1 output
17	branches, each named for the band it fires on:
18	
19	```json
20	"routing": {
21	  "kind":       "comparator",
22	  "thresholds": [3, 7, 11, 17]
23	}
24	```
25	
26	Five output ports get named `below_3`, `between_3_7`,
27	`between_7_11`, `between_11_17`, `above_17`. The single-
28	threshold case (`thresholds: [c]`) reduces to the band `[below_c,
29	above_c]` — different shape from today's three-branch lt/eq/gt.
30	To recover the lt/eq/gt semantics, **doubled thresholds** mark
31	zero-width equality bands:
32	
33	```
34	thresholds: [3, 3]         → < 3      / == 3   / > 3
35	thresholds: [3, 3, 7, 7]   → < 3 / == 3 / 3<x<7 / == 7 / > 7
36	```
37	
38	This means the comparator shipped in 233 is exactly
39	`thresholds: [c, c]` under the multi-band shape, and the editor
40	can present the single-comparand UI while storing the doubled
41	form so the dispatch layer sees one consistent representation.
42	
43	### Schema
44	
45	```json
46	"routing": {
47	  "kind":       "comparator",
48	  "thresholds": [3, 7, 11, 17]
49	}
50	```
51	
52	`thresholds` is a non-empty array of numbers. Non-decreasing
53	(doubled values are valid, decreasing values are rejected). The
54	schema also accepts the legacy single-comparand form for one
55	release as a transition aid:
56	
57	```json
58	"routing": { "kind": "comparator", "comparand": 5 }
59	```
60	
61	The editor normalises this to `thresholds: [5, 5]` on next save.
62	
63	### Branch picker (dispatch layer)
64	
65	Linear scan over thresholds; zero-width bands require equality
66	checks. For `thresholds: [t0, t1, …, t_{n-1}]`:
67	
68	```
69	value <  t0          → below_<t0>
70	value == t0 == t1    → == <t0>          (when t0 == t1)
71	t_i < value < t_{i+1}→ between_<t_i>_<t_{i+1}>
72	value > t_{n-1}      → above_<t_{n-1}>
73	```
74	
75	Doubled thresholds match equality; non-doubled boundaries match
76	the open interval. The picker is straight-line code; profiling
77	might justify a binary search if thresholds gets long, but
78	typical use is N ≤ 8.
79	
80	### Inspector UI
81	
82	Two control modes share the same dropdown selection:
83	- **Simple comparator** (the 233 UI): a single number input.
84	  Stores `thresholds: [c, c]`.
85	- **Multi-band**: a sortable list of number inputs, with `+
86	  threshold` and `× threshold` buttons. Reordering enforces non-
87	  decreasing order on save.
88	
89	A toggle between the two presentations sits next to the
90	threshold list. The "Simple" mode is the default for new
91	comparator boxes; the user opts into multi-band when they need
92	it.
93	
94	## Suggested implementation steps
95	
96	1. `src/001-schema.lua` — accept `thresholds` array as a
97	   comparator alternative to the legacy `comparand`. Validate
98	   non-decreasing.

6	## Current behavior

8	Issue 233 shipped the unified `routing` schema with three kinds —

12	The schema (`src/001-schema.lua`) rejects `kind: "randomizer"`
13	outright so we don't accumulate dead state until the rule lands.
14	
15	## Intended behavior
16	
17	A call box configured for randomizer routing fires its function
18	on every invocation and then picks a single output branch
19	uniformly at random. Two-output box with `kind: "randomizer"`
20	fires `out_0` ~50% of the time and `out_1` ~50% of the time. The
21	distribution is deterministic-given-seed but spread across
22	branches — consecutive calls do not go to consecutive branches.
23	
24	### Schema
25	
26	```json
27	"routing": {
28	  "kind":      "randomizer",
29	  "n_outputs": 4
30	}
31	```
32	
33	Output port names follow the iterator convention: `out_0` …
34	`out_<n-1>`. The schema must accept `kind: "randomizer"` and
35	require `n_outputs` to be a positive integer; reject anything
36	else.
37	
38	### Branch picker (dispatch layer)
39	
40	The slot store already owns a `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot per
41	routing-counter box (issue 302). Randomizer's picker reads and
42	increments the counter, then hashes the result before taking
43	mod n_outputs:
44	
45	```c
46	uint32_t i      = slot_read_inc(counter_slot, UINT32_MAX);
47	uint32_t branch = hash(i) % n_outputs;
48	```
49	
50	`hash` is a cheap mixing function (xorshift, FNV) — not
51	cryptographic. The point is breaking the monotonic counter so
52	adjacent invocations don't land on adjacent branches.
53	
54	### Inspector UI
55	
56	Mode dropdown gains a `randomizer` option (same row as plain /
57	comparator / iterator from issue 233). When selected, the

59	shape iterator uses today.

## Assistant

Wrote `issues/250-routing-kind-nonlinearity.md`, mirroring the format from 240–243.

The shape of the issue: schema + branch-picker + inspector sections like its siblings, but with the recognition that **this is the first routing kind that rewrites the wire value** instead of just selecting a branch — which is the most interesting architectural note in there.

A few design notes I want to flag for your decision (all also expanded as open questions in the file):

- **Auto vs fixed bounds is the most interesting axis.** Auto means non-deterministic outputs across runs (a value early in the run remaps differently than the same value late in the run, once min/max have widened). That's a real cost — debugging downstreams becomes "what did the box see before this value?" One mitigation: a "freeze observed bounds" action that snapshots auto → fixed on save.
- **Sigmoid wants something to bend.** If you sigmoid a normalised `t ∈ [0,1]` directly, the output range is roughly `[0.5, 0.73]` — barely curved. You almost always want to center the input (`t - 0.5`) and apply a steepness `k`. So the "default sigmoid" needs a default `k`, and the question is whether to expose `k` to the user or pick something opinionated (I'd lean opinionated — `k ≈ 6` gives a satisfying S — and let power users edit the JSON directly).
- **Shape choice has implications for output range.** Sigmoid is `[0,1]`, tanh is `[-1,1]`. Either pick one and let `out_range` field map between them, or let the shape dictate. The first is more flexible, the second is less surprising.
- **The first value seen under `auto`** has no `[min, max]` yet. I picked "emit 0.5" as the bootstrap; alternatives are "emit input unchanged" or "suppress the emit" (breaks the "every fire emits one value" contract every other routing kind upholds).
- **Hard-error on non-numeric input** matches your preferences exactly — no silent coercion, no skip-on-bad-input fallback. `strtod` is "good enough" but accepts `"3.14abc"` as 3.14; strict parse (reject trailing junk) is the more consistent choice.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- Generalising the dispatch layer from "routing picks a branch" to "routing may also rewrite the value" is the architectural shift this issue introduces. If you ever want **square**, **log**, **abs**, or **quantise** as routing kinds, factor that path as a first-class concept now rather than special-casing this one kind.
- The auto-mode running min/max is the first slot kind in the project (that I'm aware of) where CAS-update semantics are load-bearing on shared state. Per-worker bounds would be faster but produce drifting output streams — shared with atomic CAS is the right shape but worth knowing it's the precedent it sets.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**Which open question do you want to nail down first?** My read is the name (`nonlinearity` / `squash` / `remap`) and the bounds-mode default (`auto` vs `fixed`) are the two that have to settle before any code lands — everything else can be tuned after the first fixture runs.

    248 — input-side encapsulation: sub-maps as boxes via load-time inlining
    
    A map directory can now appear as one box in a parent map. The loader
    recognizes kind: "map" and an external block on the sub-map's data
    boxes; a new pass between load_boxes and resolve_topology splices the
    sub-map's boxes into the parent with namespaced ids, then rewires any
    parent wire that landed on the encapsulating box to flow directly to
    the matching ext-supplied data box's downstreams (preserving routing
    branch tags). The result by the time topology resolution starts is
    one flat graph with the encapsulating record left inert.
    
    Verified end-to-end with a fixture whose parent reads a literal and
    wires it into a sub-map whose write box deposits the value on disk —
    the file contains exactly what the parent sent. Output-side
    (externally-consumed write boxes surfacing as the encap's output
    ports) and editor UI are tracked as deferred on the issue.

1	# 010-graph-loader.c — public surface
2	
3	C graph loader (phase 3). Reads a map directory, parses every
4	JSON file, and produces an in-memory `graph_t` the dispatch layer
5	and pool runner consume. Replaces `src/003-loader.lua`.
6	
7	## Lifecycle
8	
9	- `graph_t *graph_load(const char *map_dir, char **err)` — read +
10	  parse + validate. Returns NULL on any failure and sets `*err` to
11	  a malloc'd `"<file>:<line>: <message>"` diagnostic. The caller
12	  frees `*err`.
13	- `void graph_destroy(graph_t *g)` — frees every byte the graph
14	  owns (the box and connection arrays, the input declarations, the
15	  underlying JSON arena holding every string).
16	
17	## Accessors
18	
19	- `const char *graph_name(g)`
20	- `const char *graph_description(g)`
21	- `const char *graph_entry_box_id(g)`
22	- `int          graph_n_boxes(g)`
23	- `const box_t *graph_box(g, i)`
24	- `const box_t *graph_box_by_id(g, id)`
25	
26	## Public types
27	
28	- `box_kind_t` — `BOX_CALL` / `BOX_READ` / `BOX_WRITE`.
29	- `routing_kind_t` — `ROUTING_PLAIN` / `ROUTING_COMPARATOR` /
30	  `ROUTING_ITERATOR`; randomizer / weighted / distributor enum
31	  values exist but the parser doesn't accept them yet.
32	- `routing_t` — `kind` plus per-kind params (`n_outputs`,
33	  `comparand`).
34	- `input_decl_t` — `name`, `type`, `literal`, `optional`.
35	- `connection_t` — outgoing connection. Stores string refs
36	  (`to_box`, `to_input`); resolved-to-integer-index forms come in
37	  the topology iteration.
38	- `box_t` — all of the above per box.
39	
40	## Schema currently enforced
41	
42	- `meta.json` must be a JSON object containing at least `name`.
43	- Every file under `boxes/` ending in `.json` is a box file with a
44	  top-level object, `id` (string), `kind` ∈ `{call, read, write}`.
45	- `call` boxes: require `ref` and `routing`. `fn` is optional (a
46	  language without function-name dispatch is fine). `lang` is
47	  optional too — falls back to inference from `ref` extension once
48	  the spec registry lands.
49	- `read` boxes (issue 229): an inline `value` literal OR a `path`
50	  field; no `ref` / `fn` / `routing`. With `value` set, the box
51	  emits the literal directly and the `path` port hides on the canvas.
52	- `write` boxes (issue 229): no kind-specific required fields beyond
53	  inputs `path` and `value`. Pushes the boolean string `"true"`
54	  downstream after a successful write.
55	- `routing.kind` ∈ `{plain, comparator, iterator}` (issue 233's
56	  shipped surface). `comparator` requires `comparand` (number or
57	  string-form number per the issue's example shape).
58	  `iterator` requires `n_outputs` (>= 1).
59	- Box ids must be unique across the map. O(n²) scan; n is small.
60	
61	## What's NOT here (deferred to follow-on iterations within 305)
62	
63	- **Phase 4 — topology validation.** Connection endpoints aren't
64	  resolved to integer indices yet; we don't verify that every
65	  `to_box` refers to a real box, nor that the `to_input` matches a
66	  declared port. Cycle detection (excluding iterator-rooted
67	  cycles) lands here too.
68	- **Phase 5 — slot size class enumeration.** The slot store's
69	  `slot_alloc` consumes a `cell_capacity`; the loader's job is to
70	  scan box outputs and enumerate the distinct sizes the graph
71	  needs.
72	- **Phase 6 — entry-box detection.** Boxes with no inputs (or
73	  inputs fed only by `data` boxes) get auto-detected as entry
74	  points.
75	- **Phase 7 — language enumeration.** Walk every call box,
76	  collect distinct `lang` values, hand the set to the spec
77	  registry.
78	- The remaining routing kinds (`randomizer`, `weighted`,
79	  `distributor`) — issue 233 deferred them to their own
80	  follow-ons; the parser rejects them with a precise message.
81	
82	None of these block issues 301 / 303 / 306 from starting.
83	
84	## Related
85	
86	- Issue 305 — design.
87	- Issue 233 — unified routing schema this loader implements.
88	- Issue 229 — data / file_write box kinds.
89	- Issue 314 — the JSON parser this depends on.
90	- Issue 302 — slot store; the loader will eventually hand size
91	  class enumeration to it.
92	
```

# scripts/run-tests.sh — phase 3 integration tests.
#
# Runs every fixture map under tests/maps/ through `soramech-pool`
# and asserts that the captured outputs match a hardcoded
# expectation per map. The point is to catch regressions
# end-to-end — past the spec interface, past the dispatch action,
# past JSONL writing — rather than via the in-process unit tests.
#
# Per the project convention: scripts run from any directory via a
# hard-coded ${DIR} path with an override argument; all paths are
# relative to ${DIR}.

fail=0
failures=()

# {{{ check_map() — run one fixture, verify expected substrings
check_map() {
    local map="$1"
    shift
    local expected=("$@")

    printf "  %-44s " "$map"

    local output
    # Per-map env opt-in: a map may set SORAMECH_TEST_WORKERS to
    # pin worker count for tests that depend on per-worker state
    # (e.g. issue 318's $lang_opaque, which lives in the producer's
    # Lua registry and can only be reconstructed by a consumer on
    # the same worker).
    local workers_env=""
    if [[ -f "$DIR/tests/maps/$map/.test_workers" ]]; then
        workers_env=$(cat "$DIR/tests/maps/$map/.test_workers")
    fi
    if [[ -n "$workers_env" ]]; then
        output=$(SORAMECH_WORKERS="$workers_env" "$DIR/soramech-pool" "$DIR/tests/maps/$map" 2>&1)
    else
        output=$("$DIR/soramech-pool" "$DIR/tests/maps/$map" 2>&1)
    fi
    local rc=$?

    local missing=""
    if [[ $rc -ne 0 ]]; then
        missing="exit=$rc"
    fi
    for e in "${expected[@]}"; do
        if [[ "$output" != *"$e"* ]]; then
            missing+="${missing:+; }missing '$e'"
        fi
    done

    if [[ -z "$missing" ]]; then
        printf "ok\n"
        pass=$((pass + 1))
    else
        printf "FAIL — %s\n" "$missing"
        fail=$((fail + 1))
        failures+=("$map: $missing")
    fi
}
# }}}

        failures+=("pipeline: $file missing")
    fi
}

Once an outer sub-map gets inlined, its inner BOX_MAP appears as a fresh entry in the parent's flat box list with the right ref, and the next iteration handles it. No code change needed; only a fixture to prove it.

The pointer-array I allocated locally got `free()`d as soon as the records inside were copied into `g->boxes` — but my new output-side splice still needed the original `sub_boxes[i]` indexing to find the ext-consumed write box. The records are still alive (they migrated to the graph), but reading them through the freed *pointer array* is UB and crashed on the first dry run. Moving the `free` after the splice fixed it. The lesson is that "the records are still owned" doesn't mean "every container I held them in is still valid" — separate lifetimes.
- The `do_write_box` change is genuinely small — three lines of new behavior inside one `if (rc == 0 && out_buf)` — because the externally-consumed semantics fit naturally into the existing return path. The write box already wrote the file and the disk-write/wire-emit pair is independent; only the bytes copied into `out_buf` had to change.

## Assistant

Wrote `issues/320-box-reconfigure-via-third-input-ring.md`. The shape: a per-box auxiliary inbox carrying box-JSON-shaped reconfigure messages, treated as a scheduling peer to the per-port input rings, gated by a yield-and-requeue barrier instead of a spinlock.

A few design notes worth flagging for your decision (also expanded as open questions in the file):

- **Per-box vs per-port ring placement.** I went with per-box because the message concerns the whole box — but the user-facing phrase "third ring" could mean per-port (mirroring the native/JSON pairing exactly). If per-port, every port could carry config and "which port's config wins?" needs answering. Per-box is cleaner; flag if you'd rather mirror per-port symmetry.
- **Scheduler ordering between value-pops and reconfigure-pops.** Three defensible rules:
  - **Strict FIFO across all four channels** using issue 318a's per-cell ordering tags — most consistent with the "interleave naturally" model.
  - **Reconfigures get priority** — drain them before any fire; every fire runs under the latest config.
  - **Reconfigures get no priority** — values in flight keep their original interpretation under the old config.
  
  Option 1 matches your phrasing best ("placed in the queue the same as all the other inputs"); option 2 is the "configuration is always current" stance; option 3 is "values keep their original interpretation."
- **Yield-and-requeue target end.** You said both "end" and "beginning" in one sentence. End-of-queue is fairer (other tasks get to run before the contended worker retries); beginning is faster recovery. I'd default to end but it's your call.
- **Scope of reconfigurable fields in slice 1.** I proposed "cheap fields (lang/ref/fn/routing/output_capacity) + connections[]; reject changes to id/kind/inputs[] with a precise diagnostic; defer the expensive port-shape changes to a follow-on." Anything missing from that scope?
- **The "not-quite-a-spinlock" name.** I called it the "yield-and-requeue barrier" in the prose. It's a barrier in the sense that it's the gate, but cooperative-with-the-scheduler rather than blocking — your phrasing made me lean away from "lock" entirely. If you have a preferred name, the issue can adopt it.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The synchronization primitive you described is unusual in C runtimes and **interesting**: instead of a thread blocking when it can't make progress, it returns to the scheduler with a "retry me later" hint. This is the same shape Go's goroutine yield uses, and what `async/await` runtimes do when a future returns `Pending`. The cost is one extra trip through the scheduler; the benefit is no busy-wait, no priority inversion, no thread parking. For SoraMech's pool-based dispatch where every fire is a small unit of work, this is genuinely the right primitive — and naming it something other than "lock" (since it isn't one) matters for keeping the mental model honest.
- This issue is the symmetric counterpart to 319: 319 grows the graph (additive — `create_box`, `connect`), 320 mutates what's already there (replacing). Together they cover the full "graph as a living artifact" surface, which is what makes the runtime feel mutable in a coherent way rather than as a pile of escape hatches.
- The "JSON exactly matching the box's own schema" choice means **the box-file parser is doing double duty** — it parses the load-time JSON files AND the runtime reconfigure messages. One parser, one validator, one schema. If you ever change the box JSON shape, both paths get the change for free. That's the same economy of design as your `external` block being a single struct used by both ext-supplied data boxes and ext-consumed write boxes — one mechanism, two destinations.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The per-port placement is conceptually stronger than per-box because it preserves the **single ordering scheme** that already governs value cells: if the producer pushes "value, value, reconfigure, value" onto a port, the consumer sees them in exactly that order. A per-box config inbox would have been a parallel scheduling channel, requiring its own ordering rules to interleave with port pops. Per-port means "one fewer thing to coordinate" — same scheduler, same FIFO, just one extra tag value.
- YARQ being **cooperative with the scheduler** rather than blocking is the move that unlocks per-cell reconfigure interleaving. A traditional lock would have meant "while reconfiguring, every other worker that touches this box stalls a thread"; YARQ means "while reconfiguring, every other worker that touches this box returns to the pool and gets used for other work." The barrier holder doesn't pay a coordination cost; the contended workers each pay one extra scheduler trip. That's a much friendlier accounting for a runtime where thousands of tiny tasks compete for tens of workers.
- The comprehensive-first-slice preference is the right call **because the cross-cutting plumbing IS the work**. Splitting "cheap fields now, port-shape changes later" would mean writing the input-gather → YARQ → reconfigure-apply pipeline twice (once for the easy case, once again with slot-store growth/shrink threaded through). Doing both in one pass means the plumbing is shaped correctly from the start — slot store calls live next to JSON parse calls live next to producer re-resolution calls, all in one function, one mental model.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

1	# Strategem — a contract must fit every implementer, not just the simplest
2	
3	## The pattern
4	
5	When designing a contract that several implementers will satisfy
6	(spec interfaces, abstract types, system protocols), check whether
7	the contract's assumptions hold for *every* class of implementer,
8	not just the cleanest case in front of you. A contract that works
9	for one class and almost-works for another is a contract that
10	forces the awkward class into shims, hacks, or special-cases. The
11	right move is to weaken the contract until it fits everyone
12	honestly.
13	
14	The trap is subtle: the cleanest implementer often comes to mind
15	first when you're designing. C and Bash specs in this project both
16	treat values as bytes — their bridges write to and read from `dst`
17	buffers. The proposed amendment to issue 312 designed the
18	dispatch-side normalisation around this: "dispatch calls the
19	consumer spec's `json_to_native` with a buffer, gets native bytes
20	back, hands them to invoke." Clean, symmetric, byte-oriented.
21	
22	The amendment failed when Lua showed up. Lua's `json_to_native`
23	doesn't write to a buffer — it pushes a value onto the worker's
24	`lua_State` stack. There is no "Lua native byte form" external
25	to the state for dispatch to hand to invoke. And Lua isn't an
26	outlier: every runtime that owns its values (Python, Ruby,
27	JavaScript, anything with a private GC heap) would have the same
28	shape. The amendment assumed buffer orientation; half of all
29	possible future specs don't have buffer orientation; the contract
30	was wrong.
31	
32	## How to apply
33	
34	When sketching a new contract:
35	
36	- List the implementers you can imagine. Not just the ones you
37	  have today — the ones a future user might bring.
38	- For each, ask: does the contract's central abstraction (bytes,
39	  callbacks, state ownership, etc.) actually fit how that
40	  implementer naturally works?
41	- If even one implementer needs a shim — "we'll just say its
42	  buffer is empty," "it'll ignore that half of the signature,"
43	  "we'll define a convention where..." — the contract is doing
44	  half the work and the implementer is doing the other half.
45	  That asymmetry is a smell.
46	- Either weaken the contract so the awkward implementer fits
47	  honestly, or accept that the contract is for a narrower
48	  category (e.g. "buffer-oriented specs only") and design a
49	  separate path for the others.
50	
51	The litmus test: can the most awkward implementer satisfy the
52	contract *without lying*? If lua_json_to_native has to set
53	`*dst_size = 0` and leave dst untouched because Lua doesn't have
54	bytes to write, the signature is forcing it to satisfy a shape
55	that doesn't apply. That's the lie. The dispatch can't actually
56	use the (empty, zero-sized) result. The contract has dead
57	parameters for half its implementers.
58	
59	## Adjacent pattern — the "agnosticism" question
60	
61	When a user asks "is this design agnostic to X?", they're usually
62	asking exactly this question. The answer to "is the system
63	agnostic to runtime statefulness?" is: yes, if and only if the
64	contract doesn't assume statelessness. Buffer-oriented bridges
65	assume statelessness. Stack-protocol bridges accommodate
66	statefulness. Neither is wrong; what's wrong is mixing them and
67	hoping the awkward case will quietly degrade.
68	
69	## Why this happens
70	
71	When the contract is being designed, the people in the room are
72	usually thinking about the implementers in front of them. Future
73	implementers don't get to participate. So the contract drifts
74	toward what works for the present implementers, and the future
75	ones inherit the asymmetry. The discipline is to imagine those
76	future implementers explicitly — to write down their shape and
77	ask if the contract fits, before shipping.
78	
79	This is especially load-bearing for plugin / extension surfaces
80	(spec interfaces, hook points, anything with a `register_X` API).
81	The whole point of those surfaces is that new implementers will
82	appear. If the contract was built for the first two, the third
83	will not fit.
84	
```

6	## Current behavior
7	
8	The routing kinds shipped or queued so far — `plain`, `comparator`,
9	`iterator`, `randomizer` (240), `weighted` (241), `distributor`
10	(242), `multi-band-comparator` (243) — all pick a **branch** and
11	forward the producer's value to the consumer **unchanged**. The
12	schema (`src/001-schema.lua`) and the dispatch picker
13	(`src/012-dispatch.c`) treat the wire payload as opaque on the
14	way out; routing has only ever decided *where* a value goes, never
15	*what* it is.
16	
17	There is no routing kind that **transforms the value** on the way
18	through. A user who wants the producer's output remapped into a
19	new numeric range — for feeding a UI slider, an audio level, a
20	heat-map cell — has to insert a dedicated call box that runs a
21	Lua / C function whose entire job is one arithmetic expression.
22	That's a lot of box for one knob.
23	
24	## Intended behavior
25	
26	A new routing kind, **`nonlinearity`** (working name; "squash"
27	is the alternative — see open questions), maps each numeric value
28	that flows through the box into a bounded output range via a
29	chosen unary function (default: logistic sigmoid). The input is
30	normalised against either:
31	
32	- **`auto`** — the running min and max observed on this wire
33	  during the current run, OR
34	- **`fixed`** — two user-supplied numeric bounds (`min`, `max`).
35	
36	After normalisation the value lands in `[0, 1]` (or `[-1, 1]` for
37	tanh — see open questions), the chosen non-linearity is applied,
38	and the result is forwarded on the box's single output port. The
39	routing kind has exactly one output — fan-out happens the same
40	way every other single-output box's fan-out happens (multiple
41	wires leaving one port).
42	
43	-- to switch between auto and fixed, the user just needs to supply one or two
44	   values - if they supply one, the minimum / maximum is set (the slots in the
45	   editor and json are specified as "min" or "max" so there's no ambiguity about

47	   I want there to be only one mode, and auto is the fallback if no fixed values

50	   the min and max value - they basically say "is this a fixed value or is it
51	   an auto value?" - if the flag is set to fixed, then the value won't change if
52	   we receive a higher/lower value. If the flag is unset to auto, then we will

57	   The vision I had, which might be more / less useful for AI purposes than some

59	   set to certain values, and whatever inputs come in will get fairly mid value
60	   unless they're very clearly a "strong" value one way or the other. This is

74	
75	### Schema
76	
77	```json
78	"routing": {
79	  "kind":     "nonlinearity",
80	  "shape":    "sigmoid",        // or "tanh" / "linear" / "softsign"
81	  "mode":     "auto",           // or "fixed"
82	  "min":      0,                // present only when mode == "fixed"
83	  "max":      100,              // present only when mode == "fixed"
84	  "out_range":"unit"            // or "signed" — see open questions
85	}
86	```
87	
88	`mode: "auto"` requires no bounds — the dispatch picker maintains
89	a running min and max in two slot-store cells (issue 302) per
90	nonlinearity box, updated atomically on each fire. `mode:
91	"fixed"` requires both `min` and `max`; schema rejects either
92	missing or `min >= max`.
93	
94	### Branch picker (dispatch layer)
95	
96	There is no branch to pick — the kind always emits on the single
97	output. The dispatch code path differs from the existing
98	routing kinds in that it **mutates the value** rather than
99	**selecting an index**. Pseudocode:
100	
101	```c
102	double x = coerce_to_number(value_in);     // hard-error path on failure
103	
104	double lo, hi;
105	if (mode == AUTO) {
106	    lo = slot_min_load(min_slot);
107	    hi = slot_max_load(max_slot);
108	    slot_min_cas_update(min_slot, x);      // best-effort widen
109	    slot_max_cas_update(max_slot, x);
110	} else {
111	    lo = box->fixed_min;
112	    hi = box->fixed_max;
113	}
114	
115	double t = (hi == lo) ? 0.5 : (x - lo) / (hi - lo);   // bootstrap case
116	
117	double y;
118	switch (shape) {
119	    case SIGMOID:  y = 1.0 / (1.0 + exp(-k * (t - 0.5))); break;
120	    case TANH:     y = tanh(k * (t - 0.5));               break;
121	    case LINEAR:   y = t;                                 break;
122	    case SOFTSIGN: y = (t - 0.5) / (1.0 + fabs(t - 0.5)); break;
123	}
124	
125	emit_number(out_port, y);
126	```

128	`k` is a steepness constant (see open questions). The bootstrap
129	case (`hi == lo`, true on the very first value seen under `auto`

140	The kind operates on numbers only. The dispatch picker tries to

1	# 315 — Reference-counted compiled-map artifacts
2	
3	## Status
4	open
5	
6	## Current behavior
7	
8	`scripts/soramech-compile.sh` from issue 309 is destructive at the
9	top:
10	
11	```bash
12	rm -rf "$COMPILED"
13	mkdir -p "$COMPILED" "$COMPILED/boxes" "$COMPILED/src" ...
14	```
15	
16	Whatever lived in `<map>/compiled/` before the rebuild is gone. If
17	another process — a long-running runner, a different shell, a
18	sibling tool that opened the artifact yesterday — had pinned to
19	that exact compiled layout (a particular `pool-runner` binary, a
20	particular `spec.so` ABI, a particular set of pre-compiled C
21	boxes), the rebuild yanks the rug. The holder either crashes,
22	silently retains stale `dlopen` handles, or starts reading new
23	files mid-flight.
24	
25	This is fine in single-user development. It stops being fine the
26	moment a SoraMech artifact is the kind of thing other programs
27	hold onto across time.
28	
29	## Intended behavior
30	
31	A compiled artifact carries its own reference count. Other
32	programs that depend on a particular build of a map are expected
33	to *acquire* a reference on startup and *release* it on shutdown.
34	When `soramech-compile` is asked to rebuild a map that has any
35	live references, it does NOT clobber the existing directory.
36	Instead it builds a sibling directory next door, leaving the
37	referenced one untouched until its holders are done with it.
38	
39	The reference count is **expected to be unreliable**. A crashing
40	holder doesn't get the chance to release; an SSH session that
41	drops doesn't either. The design accepts that staleness is the
42	common case, not the exception — every reference entry carries
43	enough metadata to be independently validated and (eventually)
44	reaped. The reference count is a hint and a courtesy, not a
45	guarantee.
46	
47	This is conceptually a copy-on-write filesystem for compiled
48	artifacts: writes (rebuilds) fork the universe when readers
49	exist; readers can keep reading the version they pinned to;
50	generations get garbage-collected when nothing observable still
51	points at them.
52	
53	## Concept
54	
55	A compiled directory contains a `.refs` file (hidden, dot-prefixed
56	so it doesn't clutter directory listings). It's append-only by
57	design — concurrent acquires never need to take a lock; concurrent
58	releases write a separate marker without rewriting the file.
59	
60	Each reference has three parts:
61	
62	1. **A date.** When the reference was acquired. Lets a janitor
63	   prune references older than some threshold even if their back
64	   pointer can't be validated.
65	2. **A back-pointer.** The identity of the holder — enough
66	   information that an outside observer can ask "is this holder
67	   still alive, and does it still want this reference?" without
68	   trusting the count alone. Concrete candidates:
69	   - process PID + start time (PID alone is not enough; PIDs
70	     recycle)
71	   - a path to a marker file the holder maintains (presence of
72	     the marker = the holder is still live and aware of the
73	     ref)
74	   - some combination (PID + a marker path)
75	3. **An opaque ref id.** A short string the holder can use later
76	   to identify *its* reference when it wants to release, so it
77	   doesn't accidentally release someone else's.
78	
79	A release writes an entry referencing the original acquire id.
80	Net live refs = acquires whose id isn't in the release set.
81	
82	## Reference file format
83	
84	A line-oriented log. Each line is one of two record types:
85	
86	```
87	acquire <id> <iso8601-date> <pid> <pid-start-time-ticks> <marker-path>
88	release <id> <iso8601-date>
89	```
90	
91	Append-only. Holders open with `O_APPEND` and write a single line
92	per operation. Atomic on POSIX as long as the line fits in
93	`PIPE_BUF` (4 KB on Linux) — well within budget for these short
94	records.
95	
96	Reading: tail through the file, build a set of acquire ids,
97	subtract release ids; remaining ids are nominally live. Then
98	validate each survivor's back pointer.
99	
100	A `.refs.lock` file is used only for compaction (rewriting the
101	log to drop matched acquire/release pairs) and for the
102	fork-to-sibling decision during compile. Steady-state reads /
103	writes don't lock.
104	
105	## Acquire / release API
106	
107	A small helper utility, probably a shell script for portability
108	since holders are written in many languages:
109	
110	```
111	scripts/soramech-ref.sh acquire <compiled-dir> [--id <id>] [--marker <path>]
112	scripts/soramech-ref.sh release <compiled-dir> --id <id>
113	scripts/soramech-ref.sh list    <compiled-dir>          # JSON, including staleness verdicts
114	scripts/soramech-ref.sh reap    <compiled-dir>          # compact + drop dead refs
115	```
116	
117	`acquire` prints the assigned id to stdout; the holder is
118	responsible for plumbing it to wherever it'll need to call
119	release. If no `--id` was supplied, the script generates one
120	(timestamp + random suffix).
121	
122	`list` walks the log and prints a JSON array of `{id, date,
123	holder, valid}` entries. Validation reads the back pointer's
124	liveness signal (PID exists & start-time matches, or marker file
125	exists).
126	
127	`reap` is destructive — it rewrites the log to remove entries
128	whose holders failed validation. Run periodically; never
129	automatically as part of compile (compile must not destroy state
130	its caller might care about).
131	
132	## Compile-time fork logic
133	
134	`soramech-compile.sh` consults `<map>/compiled/.refs` (and any
135	sibling generation directories' `.refs` files) before deciding
136	where to write:
137	
138	1. If `<map>/compiled/` doesn't exist → build there, fresh.
139	2. If it exists but has zero live references → build there, after
140	   `rm -rf`. Same destructive behavior as today.
141	3. If it exists with one or more live references → pick a sibling
142	   directory name (see below) and build there. The original
143	   `compiled/` stays intact.
144	
145	After a fork-build, the caller has a new directory; `manifest.json`
146	in the new directory records the fork relationship (`forked_from`
147	field pointing at the previous generation's path).
148	
149	### Sibling directory naming
150	
151	Two reasonable schemes; pick whichever the implementer prefers:
152	
153	- **Generation index:** `compiled.0`, `compiled.1`, `compiled.2`...
154	  Always pick `compiled.N` where N is one more than the highest
155	  existing generation. Easy to grep for; index order = build
156	  order.
157	- **Timestamp suffix:** `compiled.2026-05-19T2347` (ISO 8601
158	  compact). Order-preserving lexicographically; the name itself
159	  tells the operator when it was built.
160	
161	Whichever wins, the script should also leave a `compiled` symlink
162	pointing at the newest generation, so callers who want "the
163	latest" don't have to enumerate.
164	
165	## Stale reference handling
166	
167	A reference is stale if any of the following hold:
168	
169	- The PID no longer exists on the system.
170	- The PID exists but its start time (`/proc/<pid>/stat` field 22)
171	  doesn't match the recorded value — different process, recycled
172	  PID.
173	- The marker file path was supplied at acquire and is now
174	  missing.
175	
176	Stale refs are *tolerated*: compile-time fork still triggers if
177	ANY ref exists, stale or otherwise — the caller can run
178	`soramech-ref.sh reap` first if they want to consolidate. The
179	philosophy is: the artifact directory belongs to its readers
180	until proven otherwise, and the cost of an extra build dir is
181	trivial compared to the cost of a use-after-rebuild crash.
182	
183	## Gitignore considerations
184	
185	Every generation (`compiled/`, `compiled.0/`, `compiled.1/`,
186	`compiled.2026-05-19T2347/`, the `compiled` symlink) is a derived
187	artifact and should never be tracked. The existing
188	`.gitignore` line `tests/maps/*/compiled/` covers the canonical
189	name; add a sibling pattern to cover generations:
190	
191	```
192	tests/maps/*/compiled/
193	tests/maps/*/compiled.*/
194	```
195	
196	The `.refs` file itself lives *inside* the compiled directory,
197	so it inherits the same gitignore.
198

200

## Educational notes for 250

### Why an S-curve with a midpoint? (the math vision)

Your intuition is exactly right and exactly why neural networks use sigmoid/tanh as activation functions. Here's the underlying mechanism:

A sigmoid acts as a **soft decision boundary**. Values near the midpoint say "I have no opinion." Values far from the midpoint say "I'm confident in this direction." The shape captures the difference between *uncertainty* and *commitment* in a single function — and it does it smoothly so the gradient is continuous (which matters when you compose many of them).

When you **multiply two midpoint-0 outputs together**, you get a behavior that's structurally identical to **soft AND**:
- `0.9 × 0.9 = 0.81` (both strong positive → strong positive)
- `0.9 × -0.9 = -0.81` (disagreement → strong negative)
- `0.1 × 0.9 = 0.09` (one uncertain → uncertain)
- `0.05 × 0.05 = 0.0025` (both uncertain → very uncertain)

This is the **noise-rejection** behavior you sensed. Weak evidence doesn't accumulate into strong conclusions, because uncertainty multiplied by uncertainty stays uncertain. Strong evidence reinforces because confidence × confidence stays confident. Two boxes wired into a multiply box become a soft logic gate; chain them and you have a network of weighted votes that converges on a decision.

So your three variants map cleanly:

- **Midpoint at 0** (tanh-style, output `[-1, 1]`) — for "agree/disagree/abstain" semantics. Multiplication composes like soft AND with sign-tracking. **Best for decision-making agents** where signals have a polarity.
- **Midpoint at 0.5** (sigmoid-style, output `[0, 1]`) — for "probability/confidence" semantics. Multiplication composes like a probabilistic conjunction (assuming independence). **Best for evidence-accumulation pipelines** where everything is a likelihood.
- **No midpoint, just scaling** (linear, output `[0, 1]`) — for "calibrate this range to that range" with no decision content. **Best when you're just remapping a sensor reading** to a UI slider's range.

### How do you build intelligent behavior with this?

The mechanism is **composition**. Wire many nonlinearity boxes together, each looking at different inputs, each with its own bounds and steepness. The output of each is a confident "yes/no/abstain." Combine those outputs through multiplication (soft AND), addition followed by another nonlinearity (soft OR with re-thresholding), or weighted sums followed by a nonlinearity (the perceptron — the building block of deep learning).

An RL-style agent might use:
- Sensor box → nonlinearity (raw → confidence)
- Two confidences → multiply (soft AND)
- Many such AND-ed signals → weighted sum → another nonlinearity (decision threshold)
- Decision threshold → comparator routing → action

The reason this gets called "intelligent" is that the network of soft thresholds learns to ignore irrelevant signal combinations (they multiply to near-zero) and amplify relevant ones (they multiply to near-one), without anyone hand-coding which combinations matter.

**One question back to you**: are you building toward something more like a **neural-net-style perceptron lattice** (many sigmoids feeding weighted sums feeding more sigmoids), or more like a **bayesian/probabilistic pipeline** (sigmoids producing confidences that get conjuncted/disjuncted)? The choice changes what default shape / midpoint you'd want, because the two paradigms have different multiplication semantics.

### The dampening / equilibrium idea

This is a real technique — it's called **exponential moving average** of the bounds. Concretely:

```c
// every fire, decay both bounds slightly toward the midpoint
double mid = (min + max) / 2.0;
min = α * min + (1 - α) * mid;     // 0 < α < 1, e.g. α = 0.99
max = α * max + (1 - α) * mid;

// then if the new value extends the range, snap to it
if (x < min) min = x;
if (x > max) max = x;
```

Per-fire decay rate of `1 - α = 0.01` means the bounds halve their distance from the midpoint roughly every 70 fires. So an outlier from 1000 fires ago has decayed to ~0 influence by now, but a recent outlier still counts.

**Your minimum-gap question**: enforce it as a floor on `max - min`. If decay would bring them within `ε`, freeze decay until new values widen them. Or, equivalently: only decay when `max - min > 2ε`, so the gap never falls below `2ε`.

**Your re-calculation question**: yes, the curve gets re-computed every fire — but it's just `t = (x - min) / (max - min)`, three operations. Free. No precomputation needed.

**One question back to you**: do you want decay to be **symmetric** (both bounds pulled toward the midpoint equally) or **asymmetric** (the bound furthest from the midpoint decays faster, so a single outlier on one side decays quickly while the other side stays stable)? Asymmetric tends to feel more like "settling" because outliers don't bias the midpoint after they're gone.

### The midpoint-branch idea (your line 133-136)

Yes, this is a real and useful pattern — but I'd argue it's a **separate routing kind**, not a feature of nonlinearity. What you're describing is roughly: "comparator-with-magnitude" — split into above/below branches AND carry the magnitude through. Pros: captures direction+strength in one box, matches RL agent vocabulary. Cons: blends two concerns (which branch + transformation) and couples them.

The composition path is already clean: wire your nonlinearity to a downstream comparator. The nonlinearity gives the magnitude on the wire; the comparator splits the branches based on its midpoint. Two boxes, separate concerns, fully composable.

If you want it as one box, file it as a new kind — `directional-magnitude` or similar — rather than extending nonlinearity. Same reasoning as why the issue is for "value-transforming routing" specifically: keep each kind's job small and composable.

### The out-of-range "scaling value" idea (your line 298-301)

What you're describing sounds like **elastic bounds**: the user-supplied `min` / `max` are *initial estimates*, not hard limits. When a value exceeds them, the bounds widen to include it (same as `auto`), the curve re-computes, and the value gets normalized to its new position. No clamping, no erasure — the bounds just stretch.

This collapses cleanly into your fixed/auto-flag design:
- Both flags set (`fixed_min` AND `fixed_max`) → fixed mode, sigmoid saturates naturally on out-of-range (linear/softsign error out).
- Neither flag set → pure auto, bounds track the data.
- **One flag set** → asymmetric mode: the fixed side is a hard limit, the unset side tracks the data. Out-of-range on the fixed side is a hard error; out-of-range on the auto side just widens.

That last case is genuinely useful: "I know my values are always positive (fixed_min = 0), but I don't know how big they get (auto max)." Worth surfacing as a deliberate design point rather than an emergent property.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The reason sigmoid keeps showing up across so many different domains — neural networks, logistic regression, biological neuron models, dose-response curves in pharmacology, demand curves in economics — is that it's the simplest function that captures the abstract phenomenon of "smooth transition between two regimes." Anywhere you have soft thresholds, sigmoid is the natural fit.
- Your "AND of two sigmoids = soft AND" insight is essentially the discovery the perceptron paper (Rosenblatt, 1958) was built on. Deep learning is layers of weighted sums followed by nonlinearities. Three boxes of yours, properly wired, are one neuron. Many such triples wired into a lattice are a neural network.
- The fact that you arrived at "elastic bounds with a fixed/auto flag per side" without knowing the math is a sign the design's grain is correct — when the right primitive falls out of the requirements independently of the theory, you can usually trust the primitive.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Quick followups on 250

**Three variants by name, not by mathematician's jargon.** Yes, this is the right move — and it collapses two of your fields into one. Instead of `shape: sigmoid|tanh|linear` plus a separate `out_range: unit|signed`, just have `shape` carry an intent-named value:

- `shape: "decision"` → tanh under the hood, midpoint 0, output `[-1, 1]`. UI tooltip: "Soft + / − with clear neutral. Compose by multiplication when signals agree."
- `shape: "confidence"` → sigmoid under the hood, midpoint 0.5, output `[0, 1]`. UI tooltip: "Soft yes / no with uncertainty. Compose probabilistically."
- `shape: "calibration"` → linear remap, no midpoint, output `[0, 1]`. UI tooltip: "Pure range conversion, no curve. Use when you just want to rescale a sensor reading."

Three picks, three clear meanings. The user never has to know what tanh is.

**Symmetric vs asymmetric decay — your reframe is elegant and self-deciding.** Presence of a user-supplied midpoint IS the mode switch:
- Midpoint supplied → asymmetric (the midpoint anchors; bounds drift toward it).
- Midpoint absent → symmetric (the midpoint follows the data; both bounds drift toward each other).

No separate flag needed. The field's presence carries the meaning.

**Multi-band-comparator extension (+ button, absolute/percentage rows) belongs in 243, not 250.** The "+ button to add tiers" is a generalization of the multi-band-comparator UI, and the synced absolute/percentage rows are a UI convenience that works against any range — comparator OR nonlinearity OR anything else with bounds. If you want, I can write an update note onto 243 sketching it. The auto-min/max-tracking primitive that the percentage row reads from is the same primitive nonlinearity uses for `auto` mode — there's a small architectural insight there about factoring "tracked range" as a shared capability.

**Clamping as "certainty threshold" — yes, brilliant.** This reframes the user's `min`/`max` from "where the curve starts to saturate" into "the threshold past which I'm certain." That maps cleanly per variant:
- `confidence`: `input > max` → output = 1.0 (fully confident yes); `input < min` → output = 0.0 (fully confident no). Clamp away.
- `decision`: `input > max` → output = +1.0; `input < min` → output = −1.0. Clamp away.
- `calibration`: don't clamp (it's a remap, not a decision). Out-of-range values either extrapolate linearly or hard-error per your preference.

So clamping is a **per-variant default** rather than a separate toggle. Confidence and decision variants clamp; calibration doesn't.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The "auto-tracked range" primitive that nonlinearity's auto mode introduces is the kind of thing worth promoting to a first-class concept eventually. The multi-band-comparator's percentage row wants it; a histogram visualization box would want it; a normalization box (if you ever build one) wants it. Right now it lives inside nonlinearity, but once two boxes want the same thing, it earns its own ticket. Watch for that.
- Your reframe of "clamp = certainty threshold" is the kind of move that makes APIs feel natural. The user was probably going to clamp anyway because "values past my limits are obvious extremes"; by naming what they're already doing, the system gets a primitive that matches intuition without anyone having to memorize it.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

- **#2 — 248 editor toggles + Encapsulate action.** JS/HTML in `assets/`. I can read the existing inspector + file-browser code and make changes, but verifying needs you in a browser with the dev server.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The `count` action I added to the ref helper (beyond the issue's spec of `list` / `acquire` / `release` / `reap`) is the load-bearing piece for the compile script's fork decision. Returning JSON from `list` is great for diagnostics but bad for shell logic — parsing JSON with grep is fragile, and the compile script's question is a yes-or-no. A separate integer-emitting action means the script's check is one `[[ "$live" -eq 0 ]]` comparison instead of a regex over a JSON blob. Small API addition; big simplification at the call site.
- The PID + start-time-ticks back pointer is the cheapest reliable "is this process still the same one" verification on Linux. The PID alone is a recycling hazard (kernels reuse PIDs in days); the start-time-ticks anchor pins the identity to a specific process incarnation. Match both → "yes it's the same holder"; mismatch → "the PID got reused by something else, treat this ref as stale." No kernel calls, no parent tracking, just `/proc/<pid>/stat` parsing.
- The "compile/ vs compile.N/" naming asymmetry (the first generation is `compiled/`, forks are `compiled.1/`, `compiled.2/`) is a deliberate divergence from the issue's "symlink + always-indexed" suggestion. The reason: single-user development never forks, so the canonical name should be the canonical path, not a symlink that resolves to `compiled.0/`. The fork path only adds artifacts when the system genuinely needs them. The cost is no "latest" pointer — callers have to track which generation they want — but in practice each caller already knows which generation they acquired against, so the pointer wouldn't have helped them.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

194	  // Produces the label for a duplicated box (issue 234). If the source
195	  // already ends with "(copy)" or "(copy N)", increment N; otherwise
196	  // append "(copy)". A user duplicating "Stamp Time" gets a series:
197	  // "Stamp Time (copy)" → "Stamp Time (copy 2)" → "(copy 3)" etc.
198	  function next_copy_label(base) {
199	    const m = String(base || '').match(/^(.*?)\s*\(copy(?:\s+(\d+))?\)\s*$/);
200	    if (m) {
201	      const root = m[1];
202	      const n    = m[2] ? parseInt(m[2]) + 1 : 2;
203	      return root + ' (copy ' + n + ')';
204	    }

209	  // {{{ duplicate_box
210	  // Issue 234: clone the box's data, drop it at (wx, wy), and replay
211	  // every wire whose destination was the original. Outgoing wires are
212	  // skipped — the natural use is "I want another node fed by the
213	  // same data," not another sink for everything downstream. Self-
214	  // loops are skipped too: they're both incoming and outgoing,
215	  // which contradicts the two rules at once.
216	  async function duplicate_box(src_id, wx, wy) {
217	    const src = Boxes.boxes[src_id];
218	    if (!src) return;
219

221	    dup.id = 'box-' + Date.now().toString(36);
222	    dup.ui = dup.ui || {};
223	    dup.ui.x = Math.round(wx);
224	    dup.ui.y = Math.round(wy);
225	    dup.label = next_copy_label(src.label || src.id);
226	
227	    // Rewrite the clone's connection list to keep only incoming wires
228	    // from OTHER boxes, with to_box pointed at the new id. The source
229	    // box's side of each wire is patched below as a separate PUT.
230	    const incoming = [];

232	      if (c.to_box === src_id && c.from_box !== src_id) {
233	        incoming.push({ ...c, to_box: dup.id });
234	      }
235	    }
236	    dup.connections = incoming;
237	
238	    try {
239	      await API.put_box(dup.id, dup);
240	    } catch (e) {
241	      status_msg('duplicate error: ' + e.message, 'error');
242	      return;
243	    }
244	    Boxes.boxes[dup.id] = dup;
245	
246	    // For each duplicated wire, append a matching record onto the
247	    // source box's connections array and persist it. Without this the
248	    // wire would be invisible to the source-side scan in

1	-- Schema definitions and validators for SoraMech map files.
2	-- Validates box files, meta.json, and drivers.json against the spec
3	-- in docs/001-architecture.md. Used by both the runner and the server
4	-- before any file is written to disk.
5	
6	local DIR = "/mnt/mtwo/programs/sora/soramech"
7	
8	local M = {}
9	
10	-- {{{ valid_kinds
11	-- `call` runs a language function. `read` and `write` are dispatch-
12	-- layer IO primitives (issue 229) — `read` emits an inline literal
13	-- or file contents, `write` commits a `value` to disk and emits a
14	-- boolean done signal.
15	local valid_kinds = { call = true, read = true, write = true }
16	-- }}}
17	
18	-- {{{ valid_branches
19	-- A connection's `from_branch` field identifies which output of
20	-- the producer box this wire leaves from. The accepted values
21	-- depend on the producer's `routing.kind` (issue 233):
22	--   plain      → nil
23	--   comparator → 'lt' / 'eq' / 'gt'
24	--   iterator   → 'out_0', 'out_1', ... 'out_<n-1>'
25	-- The schema here only enforces the lexical shape — that a
26	-- branch string is either nil, one of the three comparator
27	-- branches, or `out_<digits>`. Cross-referencing the producer's
28	-- routing kind happens at the graph level in
29	-- `check_input_bindings` / `validate-map.lua`.
30	local valid_branches = { lt = true, eq = true, gt = true }
31	local function is_iterator_branch_name(name)
32	    return type(name) == "string" and name:match("^out_%d+$") ~= nil
33	end
34	-- }}}
35	
36	-- {{{ valid_routing_kinds
37	-- Issue 233's unified `routing` field. Plain is the default
38	-- shape for a call box that wants its single output fanned to
39	-- all wires. Comparator and iterator are the two routing kinds
40	-- shipped under 233. Randomizer / weighted / distributor /
41	-- multi-band-comparator have their own follow-on issues
42	-- (240–243); until those ship, the schema rejects their kind
43	-- values so we don't accumulate dead state.
44	local valid_routing_kinds = { plain = true, comparator = true, iterator = true }
45	-- }}}
46	
47	-- {{{ err
48	local function err(errors, msg)
49	    errors[#errors + 1] = msg
50	end
51	-- }}}
52	
53	-- {{{ validate_connection
54	local function validate_connection(c, i, errors)
55	    -- from_branch is nil (no comparator) or one of "lt"/"eq"/"gt"
56	    if c.from_box == nil then
57	        err(errors, "connection[" .. i .. "] missing 'from_box'")
58	    end
59	    if c.from_branch ~= nil
60	       and not valid_branches[c.from_branch]
61	       and not is_iterator_branch_name(c.from_branch) then
62	        err(errors, "connection[" .. i .. "] 'from_branch' must be nil, " ..
63	            "'lt'/'eq'/'gt' (comparator), or 'out_<n>' (iterator)")
64	    end
65	    if c.to_box == nil then
66	        err(errors, "connection[" .. i .. "] missing 'to_box'")
67	    end
68	    if c.to_input == nil then
69	        err(errors, "connection[" .. i .. "] missing 'to_input'")
70	    end
71	end
72	-- }}}
73

75	function M.validate_box(box)
76	    local errors = {}
77	    if type(box) ~= "table" then
78	        return { "box must be a table" }
79	    end
80	
81	    if box.id == nil or type(box.id) ~= "string" then
82	        err(errors, "missing or non-string 'id'")
83	    end
84	    if box.label == nil or type(box.label) ~= "string" then
85	        err(errors, "missing or non-string 'label'")
86	    end
87	    if box.kind == nil or not valid_kinds[box.kind] then
88	        err(errors, "missing or invalid 'kind' (must be 'call', 'read', or 'write')")
89	    end
90	
91	    if box.kind == "call" then
92	        -- Unified routing (issue 233). Every call box carries a
93	        -- `routing` field declaring how its single output reaches
94	        -- downstream wires. Routing kind also gates whether
95	        -- ref/fn are required: iterator is a pure routing
96	        -- primitive with no language function attached; plain
97	        -- and comparator boxes need a function to invoke.
98	        local r = box.routing
99	        local is_routing_primitive = false
100	        if r == nil then
101	            err(errors, "call box missing 'routing' field (issue 233)")
102	        elseif type(r) ~= "table" then
103	            err(errors, "'routing' must be a table")
104	        elseif type(r.kind) ~= "string" then
105	            err(errors, "'routing.kind' must be a string")
106	        elseif not valid_routing_kinds[r.kind] then
107	            err(errors, "'routing.kind' = '" .. r.kind ..
108	                "' is not one of 'plain'/'comparator'/'iterator' " ..
109	                "(other kinds belong to follow-on issues 240–243)")
110	        else
111	            if r.kind == "comparator" then
112	                if type(r.comparand) ~= "number" then
113	                    err(errors, "comparator routing requires numeric 'routing.comparand'")
114	                end
115	            elseif r.kind == "iterator" then
116	                is_routing_primitive = true
117	                if type(r.n_outputs) ~= "number"
118	                   or r.n_outputs < 1
119	                   or r.n_outputs ~= math.floor(r.n_outputs) then
120	                    err(errors, "iterator routing requires 'routing.n_outputs' to be a positive integer")
121	                end
122	            end
123	        end

126	        -- no in-loader migration). The editor or a one-off script
127	        -- rewrites old maps to the new shape; reading the old
128	        -- shape with this schema is meant to fail loudly.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The encap button on the map-picker row is the **single editor surface that closes the loop on issue 248**: without it, the only way to create an encap box was to hand-edit JSON. Hand-edited boxes work but bypass every UI safety net. With this button, the user can click a map, get an encap box pre-populated with the right port shape derived from the sub-map's own external markings, and just wire it up. The "derive ports from the sub-map's own marked boxes" step is what makes the affordance trustworthy — no double-entry, no risk of the parent's encap declaring ports the sub-map doesn't have.
- Loosening `from_branch` to accept any non-empty string was the schema change with the most reach. Before: the field was restricted to lt/eq/gt/`out_<n>` because every routing kind that used it had a fixed vocabulary. After: encapsulated maps can use it freely for named output ports. The lexical schema gives up some precision, but the precision moves to the graph-load step where it actually belongs — the loader knows the producer's kind and can verify the port name exists. The schema's job is shape, not semantics; this change honours that boundary.
- I deliberately didn't auto-clear `ref` / `fn` / `routing` when a box flips from `call` to `map` (or vice versa). The user can edit them manually afterward, and stale fields get ignored by the kind-appropriate loader path. The alternative — implicit field clearing on kind-change — risks discarding work the user wanted to preserve when they were just exploring. The "fields ignored when the kind doesn't read them" rule is a quieter and more forgiving contract than "fields wiped on transition," and it composes naturally with issue 320's reconfigure path where every field can change at runtime anyway.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**Verification needs your browser.** The schema and JS parse cleanly, the suite is green, but the actual UI rendering needs you to run the dev server, open the editor, and try the four new affordances:

1. Click a map in the picker → the new `encap` button should appear next to its name.
2. Clicking `encap` should drop a violet box on the canvas, labelled with the sub-map's name, with the right number of input + output ports.
3. Selecting a `read` or `write` box in the inspector should show the new "externally-supplied / externally-consumed" toggle + binding controls.
4. Selecting a `map` box should show the specialized inspector with ref + inputs + outputs lists.

1	# 319 — Built-in library for map self-construction
2	
3	## Status
4	open — planning stub. Several design questions need user resolution
5	before implementation can begin. See **Open design questions**
6	below.
7	
8	## Concept
9	
10	A map should be able to build more of itself while running.
11	Two built-in primitives, exposed by the runtime to every language
12	spec, are enough to bootstrap that capability:
13	
14	- **`create_box(filepath, function_name) -> box_handle`**
15	  Spawn a new box on the currently-running map. The first argument
16	  is the file holding the function the box will run; the second is
17	  the name of that function inside the file. The runtime does any
18	  build-pipeline work that's needed (compile the source, register
19	  the spec, allocate the box's input port slots) before returning
20	  a handle the caller can use to wire the box up.
21	
22	- **`connect(from_box, to_box_a, to_box_b, ...) -> bool`**
23	  Attach a wire from the single output of `from_box` to each of
24	  the destination boxes. Variadic on the destinations, since fan-out
25	  from a single producer is the common pattern. Returns true if
26	  every connection succeeded, false otherwise.
27	
28	Together these let a running map grow new sub-graphs in response
29	to runtime conditions: a planner box decides what sub-pipeline to
30	build, calls `create_box` for each node, calls `connect` to wire
31	them, and the dispatch layer picks up the new region on the next
32	push.
33	
34	## Why this shape works (and the parts that need to be checked)
35	
36	**Single-output-per-box is already the law.** Issue 218 collapsed
37	boxes to one output. Variadic destinations on `connect` is just
38	fan-out across that single output — no new concept on the wire
39	side. The variadic part of the API matches the data model.
40	
41	**`filepath + function_name` matches box JSON.** That's already how
42	language specs locate the code a box runs. The API takes the same
43	two strings the box JSON would hold.
44	
45	**Handle-as-return mirrors `data` boxes' encapsulation contract
46	(issue 248).** Encapsulated maps already expose typed handles
47	to externally-supplied inputs. A `create_box` handle is the same
48	kind of thing — a reference the caller uses to identify the box
49	in follow-up calls.
50	
51	## Open design questions
52	
53	These are real forks in the design. Each one changes what the
54	implementation looks like; none have a default answer that's
55	obviously right.
56	
57	### Q1 — When does the new box exist? — **RESOLVED: runtime growth, unified store**
58	
59	**Resolution.** The slot store grows at runtime. There is no
60	"static region" versus "dynamic region" distinction — every box
61	is a dynamic box, allocated through the same mechanism, whether
62	it was declared in `boxes/<id>.json` at graph load or created
63	by a `create_box` built-in call mid-run. Graph load becomes the
64	first user of the growth primitive rather than a separate code
65	path.
66	
67	**Why this is the right shape (not a compromise).**
68	
69	The slot store *already* needs dynamic memory at runtime for an
70	unrelated reason: a user may push 200 values into an input slot
71	before the consuming box has run even once. Ring buffer cells
72	have to be growable on the push path regardless of whether the
73	graph itself is growing. Once dynamic allocation is in the slot
74	store's hot path, gating new *box* allocation behind a separate
75	"static-only" pathway is artificial — we'd be solving the same
76	problem in two places.
77	
78	The encapsulated-map feature (248) and the same-language-merge
79	research (313) both want to *unzip* a `.map` file into the
80	runtime graph at the same level as ordinary boxes — the entire
81	point is that the runtime doesn't spawn a nested thread pool for
82	the inner graph. Unzipping requires growing the box population
83	at runtime. A unified growable store covers all three callers
84	(graph load, `create_box`, map unzipping) with one mechanism.
85	
86	**The structure: two-level chunked-append index table, no
87	static ceilings.**
88	
89	The slot store keeps a top-level array of "chunk pointers." Each
90	chunk is a fixed-size block of slot pointers. Slot bodies
91	themselves are allocated separately and pointed to from chunk
92	entries. Three layers of growth, each cheaper than the layer
93	above:
94	
95	- **Layer 1 — appending a slot inside a chunk** (most common).
96	  Atomic-increment the chunk's in-use counter; publish the slot
97	  pointer at that index. Lock-free, single-instruction-ish.
98	- **Layer 2 — adding a new chunk** (uncommon). Write a new chunk
99	  pointer into the top-level array at the next free top-level
100	  index; bump the atomic "chunks in use" counter. Lock-free.
101	- **Layer 3 — growing the top-level array** (rare; logarithmic in
102	  total slots across the run). When the top-level array itself
103	  fills, use the double-buffer-with-swap pattern: allocate a new
104	  top-level array of 2× size, copy existing chunk pointers
105	  (pointers only; chunks themselves stay put), atomically swap
106	  the top-level array pointer, defer-free the old array via
107	  refcount or epoch-based reclamation. Workers caching the old
108	  top-level pointer can finish their lookups against it — every
109	  chunk and every slot the old array references is still alive.
110	
111	**No static ceilings anywhere.** Layer 1's chunk capacity is a
112	tuning constant (cache-friendly size, e.g. 64), not a limit on
113	total slots. Layer 2's top-level capacity grows via layer 3.
114	Layer 3 has no upper bound. The user pays one extra indirection
115	on every slot access (top-level → chunk → slot), and a rare
116	double-buffer swap whose cost amortizes to zero across the run.
117	
118	**Same machinery serves three callers:** graph load (the first
119	batch of slots), `create_box` (one slot at a time during dispatch),
120	and `.map` unzipping for encapsulated maps (a burst of slots when
121	a sub-map is expanded into the runtime). All three look identical
122	to the slot store — append, append, append.
123	
124	The allocator-wide-lock-free property is preserved. Only the
125	in-use counters and the top-level swap use atomics; everything
126	on the hot read/write path stays per-slot.
127	
128	**Removal — refcount, not tombstone.** Issue 315 (compiled
129	artifact reference counting) is the safety mechanism. A box's
130	refcount goes to zero only when no other box references it as
131	producer or consumer; any worker about to use the box must hold
132	a reference that keeps the count positive. Therefore "refcount
133	reached zero" is a proof that no worker holds a stale pointer.
134	Slot indices freed at that moment are safe to reuse.
135	
136	No tombstoning required, no generation counters on handles, no
137	ABA hazard — 315's refcount discipline subsumes all three.
138	
139	**What this resolution does NOT decide:** the precise API of the
140	growth primitive on the slot store, the cache-line-aware chunk
141	size choice, and whether ring buffer *cell* growth uses
142	double-buffer-with-swap under the per-slot lock (the suggested
143	shape, since each slot already holds a lock during growth).
144	Those are implementation details for the slot store work itself,
145	not the `create_box` / `connect` design.
146	
147	### Prerequisite — remove the dispatch input cap before `create_box` ships
148	
149	Today `src/012-dispatch.c` allocates five parallel stack arrays
150	of size 16 (`bufs`, `buf_chunks`, `datas`, `sizes`,
151	`input_native`) inside the per-call invocation path. A box with
152	more than 16 inputs hits a hard error from the dispatcher. This
153	contradicts the "no static ceilings" principle resolved in Q1.
154	
155	**Fix:** convert the five arrays to VLAs (`char *bufs[n];` etc.,
156	C99). Cost is zero — VLAs adjust the stack pointer by
157	`n * 5 * sizeof(void*)` with no allocator call. Keep a sanity
158	guard at a generous ceiling (e.g. 4096 inputs) so a runaway
159	loader can't blow the stack; the existing error-return path
160	stays in place above that.
161	
162	**Related but lower priority:** the `branch[24]` stack buffers
163	at dispatch.c:629/647/678 hold a `snprintf("out_%u", ...)`
164	result. Worst-case formatted length is 15 bytes; 24 is
165	arbitrary-but-safe and `snprintf` truncates without overflowing.
166	Change to a named constant (`MAX_BRANCH_NAME = 16`) for hygiene
167	when the VLA work lands. Not a real bug.
168	
169	### Q1.5 — The shape of the `create_box` argument: box JSON schema as the contract
170	
171	`create_box`'s argument is **one structured value whose shape is
172	exactly the box JSON schema**. In Lua, a table; in C, either a
173	struct or a JSON string built by the caller; in Bash, a JSON
174	string. The runtime converts to JSON internally (same path as the
175	universal wire format), validates against the box schema, and
176	instantiates the box record. Anything you can write into
177	`boxes/<id>.json` on disk, you can pass to `create_box` at
178	runtime.
179	
180	**Why this shape (not a fat positional signature, not key/value
181	varargs, not a builder pattern):**
182	
183	- The box JSON schema **is** the source of truth on disk. Having
184	  `create_box` mirror that schema means there is no parallel
185	  "create_box parameter list" to maintain — adding a new schema
186	  field works in `create_box` automatically.
187	- New customization toggles (priority, debug-instrumentation
188	  flags, custom translation specs per port, emoji labels for tap
189	  mode, etc.) land in the schema and become available to
190	  `create_box` callers in the same change.
191	- Languages without rich native structured types (Bash) can use
192	  JSON strings; languages with rich types (Lua tables, C structs)
193	  can use native shapes that the spec converts.
194	
195	**Structural metadata vs runtime values — the split this design
196	enforces.** The argument carries **structural metadata** (id,
197	kind, lang, ref, fn, routing, inputs/outputs schema, position).
198	Per-invocation **runtime values** (the data flowing through
199	wires) keep flowing through input slots as before. They do not
