1976	/* {{{ Runtime mutation — box_add_connection() (issue 319d)
1977	 *
1978	 * Appends one connection to box `b`'s connections array via the
1979	 * same copy-and-publish discipline used for boxes: allocate a
1980	 * new connections[] sized current+1, copy the old in, append the
1981	 * new connection, atomic-store the new connections pointer, then
1982	 * atomic-store the new count. The old connections array is parked
1983	 * on stale_box_arrs (the list is generic, not box-specific) and
1984	 * freed at graph_destroy. */
1985	int box_add_connection(graph_t *g, box_t *b, connection_t conn)
1986	{
1987	    if (!g || !b) return -1;
1988	    pthread_mutex_lock(&g->graph_mu);
1989	
1990	    int n_old = atomic_load_explicit(&b->n_connections, memory_order_relaxed);
1991	    connection_t *old = atomic_load_explicit(&b->connections, memory_order_relaxed);
1992	
1993	    connection_t *new_conns = malloc((size_t)(n_old + 1) * sizeof(connection_t));
1994	    if (!new_conns) { pthread_mutex_unlock(&g->graph_mu); return -1; }
1995	    if (old && n_old > 0) {
1996	        memcpy(new_conns, old, (size_t)n_old * sizeof(connection_t));
1997	    }
1998	    new_conns[n_old] = conn;
1999	
2000	    if (old) {
2001	        struct stale_arr *st = malloc(sizeof *st);
2002	        if (!st) { free(new_conns); pthread_mutex_unlock(&g->graph_mu); return -1; }
2003	        st->ptr  = old;
2004	        st->next = g->stale_box_arrs;
2005	        g->stale_box_arrs = st;
2006	    }
2007	
2008	    atomic_store_explicit(&b->connections,   new_conns, memory_order_release);
2009	    atomic_store_explicit(&b->n_connections, n_old + 1, memory_order_release);
2010	
2011	    pthread_mutex_unlock(&g->graph_mu);
2012	    return 0;
2013	}

274	/* {{{ dispatch_spawn() */
275	void dispatch_spawn(const dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, int box_id, int priority)
276	{
277	    if (!ctx || !ctx->pool) return;
278	
279	    /* Task structs come from the unified allocator's free-list so
280	     * hot graphs don't pay per-spawn malloc bookkeeping. The chunk
281	     * is stashed on the task itself so dispatch_action can release
282	     * it via ua_unref without a lookup. */
283	    ua_t *heap = slot_store_allocator(ctx->slots);
284	    ua_chunk_t *chunk = ua_alloc(heap, sizeof(dispatch_task_t));
285	    if (!chunk) return;
286	    dispatch_task_t *t = (dispatch_task_t *)ua_data(chunk);
287	    t->chunk = chunk;
288	    t->live_wire_count = 0;
289	
290	    /* Assign task_id at submission so the same id correlates the
291	     * task_submit / task_start / task_end events. The next_task_id
292	     * counter is atomic so concurrent spawners don't collide. */
293	    dispatch_ctx_t *mctx = (dispatch_ctx_t *)ctx;
294	    t->task_id = atomic_fetch_add_explicit(&mctx->next_task_id, 1,
295	                                           memory_order_relaxed);
296	    t->box_id  = box_id;
297	    t->ctx     = ctx;
298	
299	    if (ctx->events) {
300	        const box_t *b = graph_box(ctx->graph, box_id);
301	        event_queue_task_submit(ctx->events, now_secs(),
302	            t->task_id, b ? b->id : "(unknown)", -1);
303	    }
304	    pool_spawn(ctx->pool, dispatch_action, t, priority);
305	}

317	     * They never enter the pool — their consumers read the cached

319	    if (b && b->kind == BOX_READ) return;

231	/* {{{ box_is_ready() — every required input has a value or fallback
232	 *
233	 * A port is satisfied when:
234	 *   - it is optional, OR
235	 *   - its slot currently holds a value, OR
236	 *   - it has at least one read-box predecessor (issue 244 — the
237	 *     consumer can pull the cached value at attempt time even
238	 *     though the slot is empty). */
239	static int box_is_ready(const dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, int box_id)
240	{
241	    const box_t *b = graph_box(ctx->graph, box_id);
242	    if (!b) return 0;
243	    if (b->n_inputs == 0) return 1;
244	    if (!b->input_slot_ids) return 0;        /* runtime not attached */
245	    for (int i = 0; i < b->n_inputs; i++) {
246	        if (b->inputs[i].optional) continue;
247	        if (slot_has_value(ctx->slots, b->input_slot_ids[i])) continue;
248	        if (b->n_read_predecessors && b->n_read_predecessors[i] > 0) continue;
249	        return 0;
250	    }
251	    return 1;
252	}

255	/* {{{ box_pop_ready() — every POP input has at least one cell */
256	/* For multi-spawn boxes, we want to re-spawn so long as every POP
257	 * input still has a queued value. PEEK inputs are always available
258	 * after their initial push, so they don't gate continuation. */
259	static int box_pop_ready(const dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, int box_id)
260	{
261	    const box_t *b = graph_box(ctx->graph, box_id);
262	    if (!b || !b->input_slot_modes) return 0;
263	    int saw_pop = 0;
264	    for (int i = 0; i < b->n_inputs; i++) {
265	        if (b->input_slot_modes[i] != SLOT_MODE_POP) continue;
266	        if (b->inputs[i].optional) continue;
267	        saw_pop = 1;
268	        if (!slot_has_value(ctx->slots, b->input_slot_ids[i])) return 0;
269	    }
270	    return saw_pop;

1931	/* {{{ Runtime mutation — graph_add_box() (issue 319d)
1932	 *
1933	 * Appends a pre-built box to the graph's pointer index. The pointer
1934	 * array grows via copy-and-publish (allocate at 2x capacity, memcpy
1935	 * the old pointers in, atomic-store the new array, park the old on
1936	 * stale_box_arrs for destroy-time reclamation). The new box's count
1937	 * is published last with release semantics so a reader seeing
1938	 * count = N also sees box N-1 fully published into the index. */
1939	int graph_add_box(graph_t *g, box_t *box)
1940	{
1941	    if (!g || !box) return -1;
1942	    pthread_mutex_lock(&g->graph_mu);
1943	
1944	    uint32_t n   = atomic_load_explicit(&g->n_boxes,      memory_order_relaxed);
1945	    uint32_t cap = atomic_load_explicit(&g->box_capacity, memory_order_relaxed);
1946	
1947	    if (n + 1u > cap) {
1948	        uint32_t new_cap = cap == 0 ? 16u : cap * 2u;
1949	        box_t **new_boxes = calloc((size_t)new_cap, sizeof(box_t *));
1950	        if (!new_boxes) {
1951	            pthread_mutex_unlock(&g->graph_mu);
1952	            return -1;
1953	        }
1954	        box_t **old_boxes = atomic_load_explicit(&g->boxes, memory_order_relaxed);
1955	        if (old_boxes && n > 0) {
1956	            memcpy(new_boxes, old_boxes, (size_t)n * sizeof(box_t *));
1957	        }
1958	        struct stale_arr *st = malloc(sizeof *st);
1959	        if (!st) { free(new_boxes); pthread_mutex_unlock(&g->graph_mu); return -1; }
1960	        st->ptr  = old_boxes;
1961	        st->next = g->stale_box_arrs;
1962	        g->stale_box_arrs = st;
1963	        atomic_store_explicit(&g->boxes,        new_boxes, memory_order_release);
1964	        atomic_store_explicit(&g->box_capacity, new_cap,   memory_order_release);
1965	    }
1966	
1967	    box_t **boxes = atomic_load_explicit(&g->boxes, memory_order_relaxed);
1968	    boxes[n] = box;
1969	    atomic_store_explicit(&g->n_boxes, n + 1u, memory_order_release);
1970	
1971	    pthread_mutex_unlock(&g->graph_mu);
1972	    return (int)n;

Suite green at 27 passed / 0 failed — a project-first as far as I can tell from the prior 4-fail baseline. Marked task #4 complete.

**Honest report on what happened with 319:**

The parent issue's `## Open design questions` is fully resolved — every Q (Q1, Q1.5, Q2, Q3, Q4, Q5) carries a **RESOLVED** marker with the chosen shape spelled out. The implementation work is also done in six completed sub-issues 319a–319f (slot store growth, dispatch cap removal, box id + compile cache, the create_box/connect builtins, C/Bash bindings, and the language-agnostic dispatch box-kinds).

The release-blocker status was about the **four failing integration tests** that segfaulted every time you ran them. So I dug in:

1. Reproduced reliably — 8/8 runs crashed with exit=139 after "run complete" prints (so the segfault was during teardown).
2. Traced `push_to_downstream` → the new connection IS visible to the trigger's fan-out with correct `to_box_idx=2, to_input_idx=0`.
3. Traced `push_one_connection` → `dst='auto_00000000' input_slot_ids=NULL → SKIP`. The new box's `input_slot_ids` field reads as NULL at the moment the trigger tries to push to it.
4. Traced `runtime_create_box` itself → `input_slot_ids=0x7f5fa80071d0`. The field was correctly populated when the box was created. So somewhere between create-time and push-time, the read was returning NULL.

Then I removed all the traces to restore the original code, rebuilt — and **the tests started passing 30/30 reliably**. Re-ran the full suite: 27/0.

**The 319 tests now pass, but I haven't actually fixed the source-level bug.** The only code diff from where I started this session is my 248 ext-consumed write-box dispatch change (which the 319 tests don't exercise). My best guess: the new branching in `do_write_box` shifted instruction layout enough to mask a latent timing-sensitive race in the runtime_create_box → push_one_connection sequence. Add a single line elsewhere in dispatch.c and the bug might come back.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The most suspicious code-level smell is in `push_one_connection`: `const box_t *dst = graph_box(...); if (!dst->input_slot_ids) return 0;` reads through a `const` pointer to a struct field that's *not* declared atomic. If the compiler is allowed to cache that field load across function calls (and `const` plus aggressive inlining can encourage that), it might be reading a stale NULL from when the box was first calloc'd, before the population loop ran. The proper fix would be to either make `input_slot_ids` `_Atomic`, or add an explicit `atomic_thread_fence(memory_order_acquire)` after the `graph_box` call. **Until that fence lands, the green status of these tests is build-fragile.**
- The pthread_mutex in `graph_add_box` is a full memory barrier on unlock, so cross-thread visibility is correct. The race lives in the SAME-thread case: trigger's worker creates the box, immediately publishes a connection to it, immediately fans out its return value to the connection — all on one thread. Same-thread visibility should be free, but the compiler's optimizer can defeat it through aggressive const-cache or inlining. This is the same class of bug as a `volatile` mistake from the 1990s; the modern answer is `_Atomic` typing, not "rely on the compiler being conservative."
- The fact that adding ANY fprintf made the tests pass is the textbook signature of this kind of bug. fprintf is a function call the compiler can't see through, so it acts as a compiler barrier, forcing the optimizer to write back caches and re-read fields after the call. That's why "add a printf and it works" is the universal C race-detection folklore.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**Recommended follow-up issue** (not in this session): "319 — harden the same-thread visibility of runtime-created box fields." Add `_Atomic` to `input_slot_ids` and `n_inputs` on box_t, plus matching atomic accessors. The current green tests would still pass; the latent race would stop being a layout-dependent ghost.

1	# 311 — Integration tests & run output (`last-run.json`)
2	
3	## Status
4	open
5	
6	## Current behavior
7	
8	Phase 2 writes a `last-run.json` after every map run, recording per-
9	box invocations, inputs, outputs, and any errors. The editor reads
10	it to display a run summary. Phase 2 testing is ad-hoc: a few maps
11	in `maps/` (`hello`, `branch-test`, `classify-demo`, `driver-test`)
12	that the developer runs by hand to verify the synchronous executor
13	still works.
14	
15	Phase 3 changes the shape of the problem: many concurrent
16	invocations, possibly thousands per run when iterators are in play,
17	written from multiple worker threads. The phase 2 "build a single
18	table at end of run" approach does not survive that. And the
19	existing maps cover only a small slice of the new surface (no
20	queued inputs, no large iterator counts, no fan-in).
21	
22	This issue covers two things that go together: the format and
23	writer for the run output, and the integration test plan that
24	exercises the phase 3 runtime end-to-end.
25	
26	## Part A — Run output
27	
28	### Decoupling from the editor
29	
30	The editor (phase 2) is being scoped down to a pure map editor — it
31	does not know how to run maps and does not display run results.
32	`last-run.json` is therefore not a UI feed. It exists for:
33	
34	- LLM consumption — agents reading the file to understand what a
35	  run did
36	- CLI-driven inspection — a future viewer utility (out of scope
37	  here) that pretty-prints the file
38	- Test harness consumption — the integration tests below diff the
39	  written file against expected output
40	
41	Decoupling means the writer's design is driven by these consumers,
42	not by editor rendering needs.
43	
44	### File format: JSON Lines
45	
46	The phase 2 single-document format does not work when the runner is
47	streaming events from many threads. Use JSON Lines instead — one
48	JSON object per line, each line is one event, the file grows
49	monotonically as the run proceeds.
50	
51	Event types:
52	
53	```jsonl
54	{"event":"run_start", "ts":1234567890.123, "map":"maps/classify-demo", "n_workers":16}
55	{"event":"task_submit", "ts":..., "task_id":42, "box_id":"classify", "worker_idx":-1}
56	{"event":"task_start", "ts":..., "task_id":42, "worker_idx":3}
57	{"event":"task_end", "ts":..., "task_id":42, "worker_idx":3, "duration_us":127, "output_size":12}
58	{"event":"slot_alloc", "ts":..., "slot_id":5, "size":256, "n_cells":1}
59	{"event":"slot_free", "ts":..., "slot_id":5}
60	{"event":"run_end", "ts":..., "duration_us":1850, "n_tasks":7}
61	```
62	
63	JSONL is append-only, which makes thread-safe writing tractable: a
64	single mutex around the write call serializes the lines, and each
65	line is self-contained so a partial line on crash is recoverable
66	(reader skips the broken trailing line).
67	
68	The reader (LLM, viewer, test harness) parses one line at a time;
69	total file size doesn't have to fit in memory.
70	
71	### What gets logged
72	
73	Per-task: submission, start, end, duration, output size. Inputs
74	and outputs are NOT logged by default — for iterator boxes
75	producing thousands of invocations, logging every value bloats
76	the file unbounded. There is a verbosity switch:
77	
78	- `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1` — log inputs and outputs (truncated past
79	  some byte limit, e.g. 4 KB) per task. For debugging.
80	- Default: log task lifecycle but not values.
81	
82	Slot allocator events (alloc, free, coalesce, grow) at a separate
83	verbosity level. Off by default; on under `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1`.
84	For diagnosing memory issues.
85	
86	### Writer mechanism
87	
88	A single dedicated writer thread inside the runner consumes events
89	from a multi-producer single-consumer ring buffer. Worker threads
90	push event records (small fixed-size structs) into the ring; the
91	writer pulls them, serializes to JSON, and writes lines to the
92	file. This avoids per-event mutex contention — the ring buffer is
93	the only shared state, and a well-written MPSC ring is lock-free
94	on the producer side.
95	
96	Alternative considered: each worker writes its own log file, merge
97	at end. Simpler concurrency, but readers would have to merge by
98	timestamp — and any cross-event reasoning (was task A still
99	running when task B ended?) requires the merge anyway.
100	
101	The writer thread is started after the pool is created and joined
102	before `pool_destroy`. It also handles `run_end` as the very last
103	event, including the final summary.
104	
105	### File location
106	
107	`<map-dir>/last-run.jsonl` (note: `.jsonl` not `.json` — the
108	extension reflects the format change). Overwritten on every run.
109	
110	A rotated archive (`last-run.jsonl.1`, `.2`, …) is out of scope.
111	Users who want history copy the file before re-running.
112	
113	## Part B — Integration tests
114	
115	### Scope
116	
117	End-to-end tests of the pool runner against real map directories.
118	Each test is:
119	
120	1. A map directory under `tests/maps/<name>/`
121	2. An expected `last-run.jsonl` (or a comparison spec) under
122	   `tests/expected/<name>.jsonl`
123	3. A test driver script that runs the map and diffs
124	
125	The test driver is `scripts/run-tests.sh`. It iterates
126	`tests/maps/`, runs each, diffs against expected (with a normalizer
127	that drops timestamps, durations, worker indices — anything non-
128	deterministic), and reports pass/fail.
129	
130	### Test maps
131	
132	Coverage targets:
133	
134	| Test map                  | What it exercises                                    |
135	|---------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
136	| `hello`                   | Single Lua box, one input, one output                |
137	| `data-only`               | Data box → call box. No inputs, just stored values   |
138	| `fan-out-3`               | One output → three consumer boxes (peek, refcount)   |
139	| `fan-in-iterator`         | Three producers → iterator with queued input         |
140	| `comparator-routing`      | Comparator with all three branches (lt/eq/gt)        |
141	| `iterator-100`            | Iterator with 100 input values, round-robin to 3 paths |
142	| `multilang`               | One Lua box, one C box, one Bash box, all wired      |
143	| `large-output`            | Box producing a 1 MB string (variable-size heap)     |
144	| `cycle-detector-fail`     | Non-iterator cycle — load must abort                 |
145	| `missing-input-fail`      | Connection references a nonexistent box — load aborts|
146	| `box-error-fail`          | Box function returns nonzero — runner aborts         |
147	
148	The `*-fail` tests verify error behavior — the runner is expected
149	to exit nonzero with a precise error message. The driver matches
150	exit code and stderr against expected.
151	
152	### Test driver
153	
154	```bash
155	# scripts/run-tests.sh
156	for test_dir in tests/maps/*/; do
157	    name=$(basename "${test_dir}")
158	    expected="tests/expected/${name}.jsonl"
159	
160	    actual=$( "${SOURCE_DIR}/soramech-pool" "${test_dir}" )
161	    rc=$?
162	
163	    if [ -f "${expected}.exit" ]; then
164	        # *-fail tests: assert exit code and stderr substring
165	        check_failure "${name}" "${rc}" "${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl"
166	    else
167	        # success tests: diff normalized last-run.jsonl
168	        check_success "${name}" "${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl" "${expected}"
169	    fi
170	done
171	```
172	
173	`normalize_jsonl` strips timestamps, durations, worker indices,
174	slot ids, and task ids (all non-deterministic) and sorts events by
175	event type. The result should be deterministic across runs.
176	
177	### Phase 3 demo map
178	
179	A single map under `issues/completed/demos/phase-3/` that

181	
182	- Multiple entry-point data boxes
183	- Lua, C, and Bash boxes all wired together
184	- An iterator with a queued input
185	- A comparator routing into different downstream paths
186	- A large-output box (variable-size heap)
187	- Non-trivial graph topology (≥ 10 boxes)
188	
189	Run with `./run.sh` from the demo directory. Prints a short summary
190	of what happened (parsing the `last-run.jsonl`) so the demo is
191	visible without a viewer utility.
192	
193	This satisfies the standing project rule (CLAUDE.md) that each
194	phase produces a runnable demo in `issues/completed/demos/`.
195	
196	### Test infrastructure constraints
197	
198	- Tests must not depend on the editor or any HTTP server
199	- Tests must not depend on internet access
200	- Tests must run in under 60 seconds total on a developer machine

## Assistant

Two new commits on top of the closeout series — the fixup that lands the missing "complete" status text into the three completed/ files, and the 311 instrumentation slice that gives 319's latent race a JSONL-visible signature. Working tree stays clean except for your pre-existing untracked WIP.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The earlier `git mv` bug is one of those silent traps: `git mv source dest` stages a rename *based on the file's last-committed content* and moves the working file. If you have unstaged modifications on `source` when you run `git mv`, the rename captures HEAD content and your modifications sit unstaged on the destination path. The right pattern is `git add source` (stage the modification) THEN `git mv source dest` — or, equivalently, `git mv source dest` then `git add dest` to stage the modification on top. The closeout commits committed clean renames with stale content; the fixup commit lands the actual intent. Worth remembering as a generic git-hygiene rule.
- The 319 latent race now has a **JSONL signature** rather than a fprintf-and-rebuild diagnosis loop. If it ever resurfaces, the transcript will literally show `{"event":"push", ..., "result":"input-slots-null"}` — no source code change needed to recognise it. That's exactly the kind of "make the bug visible from the log alone" payoff that justifies adding instrumentation events even when they don't drive a feature directly. The push-event design captures *every* skip reason as a distinct string, not just the one we care about, so other future races (`dst-null`, `to-input-out-of-range`) get the same diagnostic treatment for free.
- The split between **always-emit mutation events** (box_create, wire_add, runtime slot_alloc) and **opt-in per-push events** (`SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1`) is the right verbosity boundary. Mutations are O(graph edits), which the user controls and which are load-bearing for any audit log. Pushes are O(every wire fire), which is unbounded — gating them behind an env var keeps default runs cheap while making deep diagnosis one env var away.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

1	# 241 — Routing kind: weighted
2	
3	## Status
4	open · design carried forward from issue 233
5	
6	## Current behavior
7	
8	Issue 233 shipped the unified `routing` schema with three kinds —
9	`plain`, `comparator`, `iterator`. The dispatch layer
10	(`src/012-dispatch.c`) reserves an enum slot for `weighted` and
11	falls it through to plain; the schema rejects the kind value
12	until this issue lands.
13	
14	## Intended behavior
15	
16	Weighted routing picks a branch by probability. With a two-
17	output box and weights `[0.8, 0.2]`, ~80% of invocations fire
18	`out_0` and ~20% fire `out_1`. The distribution is deterministic-
19	given-seed because the counter advances per invocation, but the
20	mapping from counter to branch is the weighted band lookup, not
21	modulo.
22	
23	### Schema
24	
25	```json
26	"routing": {
27	  "kind":    "weighted",
28	  "weights": [0.8, 0.2]
29	}
30	```
31	
32	`weights` is an array of non-negative numbers; their sum should
33	be 1.0 (the schema renormalises silently if not — see open
34	questions). The output port count is `weights.length`, with the
35	same `out_<i>` naming.
36	
37	### Branch picker (dispatch layer)
38	
39	At compile time the loader normalises weights into a cumulative
40	table on an integer precision scale (e.g. 1000):
41	
42	```
43	weights [0.8, 0.2]  →  cumulative [800, 1000]
44	weights [1, 1, 2]    →  cumulative [250, 500, 1000]   (normalised)
45	```
46	
47	Per call:
48	
49	```c
50	uint32_t r      = slot_read_inc(counter_slot, PRECISION);
51	uint32_t branch = lookup_band(r, cumulative_table);
52	```
53	
54	Same `SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER` slot machinery as iterator and
55	randomizer; only the table lookup differs.
56	
57	### Inspector UI
58	
59	The mode dropdown gains a `weighted` option. The per-kind
60	control is a horizontal slider with N-1 knobs dividing the bar
61	into N segments. One line per output port below the slider
62	shows a visual band with the port's percentage:
63	
64	```
65	out_0    [████████░░░░░░░░░░░░]    80%
66	out_1    [░░░░░░░░████████████]    20%
67	```
68	
69	Adjusting a knob updates the percentages live; percentages are
70	also editable directly (typing `30` into the right column
71	shifts the relevant knob and renormalises the others).
72	
73	## Suggested implementation steps
74

1	# 242 — Routing kind: distributor (load-aware)
2	
3	## Status
4	open · design carried forward from issue 233
5	
6	## Current behavior
7	
8	Issue 233 shipped the unified `routing` schema. `distributor` is
9	reserved as an enum value in `src/012-dispatch.c` but falls
10	through to plain; the schema rejects the kind until this issue
11	lands.
12	
13	## Intended behavior
14	
15	Distributor routing sends the function's output to the
16	**least-busy** downstream consumer. The dispatch action inspects
17	the fill level of every input slot wired to each branch and
18	picks the branch whose downstream slot has the fewest queued
19	values.
20	
21	### Schema
22	
23	```json
24	"routing": {
25	  "kind":      "distributor",
26	  "n_outputs": 3
27	}
28	```
29	
30	Same `out_<i>` port naming and `n_outputs` count as the other
31	counter-driven kinds.
32	
33	### Branch picker (dispatch layer)
34	
35	Unlike the counter-driven kinds, distributor reads downstream
36	state at dispatch time:
37	
38	```c
39	uint32_t best_branch = 0;
40	uint32_t best_fill   = UINT32_MAX;
41	for (int i = 0; i < n_outputs; i++) {
42	    uint32_t fill = downstream_fill(box, i);
43	    if (fill < best_fill) { best_branch = i; best_fill = fill; }
44	}
45	// tie-breaker: atomic counter, so ties don't always go to branch 0
46	if (count_ties(box, best_fill) > 1) {
47	    best_branch = slot_read_inc(tiebreaker_slot, n_outputs);
48	}
49	```
50	
51	`downstream_fill(box, i)` reads `tail - head` on the slot wired
52	to `out_<i>`. The slot store already exposes
53	`slot_fill_count` per issue 302.
54	
55	For fan-out (one branch with multiple consumers), the design
56	question is whether to use max, sum, or mean of the consumer
57	fills. Issue 233 leans toward **max** — bottleneck is the
58	slowest consumer.
59	
60	### Inspector UI
61	
62	Mode dropdown gains `distributor`. The per-kind control is the
63	same `n_outputs` number input the iterator and randomizer use.
64	
65	## Suggested implementation steps
66	
67	1. `src/001-schema.lua` — accept `kind: "distributor"`,
68	   validate `n_outputs`.
69	2. `src/012-dispatch.c` — implement the picker. Tie-breaker
70	   uses a counter slot the box already has from issue 302.
71	3. `src/009-slot-store.c` — verify `slot_fill_count` is
72	   available cheaply (already shipped per 302 unit tests).
73	4. `assets/js/004-inspector.js` — add `distributor` to the
74	   dropdown, reuse iterator's `n_outputs` control.
75	5. `assets/js/002-boxes.js` — `out_<i>` rendering already
76	   covers it.
77	6. Fixture: `tests/maps/distributor-route/` — three downstream
78	   sinks with different inherent latencies, send N inputs
79	   through the distributor, assert the slow sink received
80	   fewer than the fast ones.
81	
82	## Relevant files
83	
84	- `issues/completed/233-unified-routing-schema.md` — parent.
85	- `issues/302-wire-value-slot-store.md` — `slot_fill_count`
86	  this picker calls.
87	- `src/012-dispatch.c` — dispatch table.
88	- `assets/js/004-inspector.js`, `assets/js/002-boxes.js` —
89	  editor side.
90	
91	## Open questions
92	
93	- **Fan-out fill semantics**: max vs sum vs mean of downstream
94	  consumers when a branch fans to multiple boxes. Issue 233
95	  leans max; revisit if a workload says otherwise.
96	- **Sampling cost**: reading every downstream slot's fill on
97	  every invocation is O(n_outputs × fan_out_per_branch). For
98	  N=3 that's negligible; for N=32 with deep fan-out it could
99	  matter. Defer optimisation until a profile demands it.
100	- **Empty-everywhere case**: every downstream slot has 0
101	  fill. Pick branch 0? Round-robin via the tie-breaker?
102	  Round-robin is what the design specifies and is the right
103	  answer — no branch is "more empty" than any other.
104

11	# $(DIR) per the project convention.

15	# exist under src/, libs/task-pool/, and libs/json/, so it scales as
16	# those issues land.

#
# Produces spec.so, a small .so the pool runner dlopens at startup.

# pass the project root so the -I path to langs/lang-spec.h resolves.

# {{{ Resolve project root
DIR ?= $(abspath $(dir $(lastword $(MAKEFILE_LIST)))/../..)

The 240 commit deliberately bundles the multi-kind editor surface (schema + canvas + inspector dropdown + per-kind controls + setters) since splitting interleaved JS hunks per-issue would create more friction than value; the 241/242/243 commits each carry just the fixture, the run-tests entry, the phase-2-progress row, and the move-to-completed for their own issue. 243 also carries its C-side work (the thresholds field + parsing + dispatch picker + MAX_BRANCH_NAME bump). The 319 issue file got a corrected postscript: what I'd flagged as a latent visibility race turned out to be a partial-rebuild trap in the Makefile, now closed by `-MMD -MP` auto-deps.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The Make bug had been **silently corrupting struct reads for three or four sessions** every time we extended `box_t` or `routing_t`. Every "intermittent" 319 failure I saw, every "fixed by adding traces" mystery, every "clean rebuild made it work" — all the same root cause. Auto-header-deps is the kind of infrastructure that pays for itself the first time it prevents a wild-goose chase, and the diagnostic JSONL events from 311's earlier commit are what made it diagnosable at all (the push event's `result=to-input-out-of-range` was the breadcrumb that pointed at field-offset corruption rather than memory ordering).
- The `DIR := $(abspath ...)` immediate-assignment fix is the kind of make footgun that bites quietly: with `?=` recursive, `$(MAKEFILE_LIST)` changes every time `-include` pulls in another file, so `$(dir lastword ...)` silently mutates between expansions. The compile command's `-I/.../build/src/langs` (a path that doesn't exist) was the only visible symptom — and only when a header search actually missed. The dry-run `make -n` caught it immediately because it printed the actual cc command; without that the error message blamed lang-spec.h.
- Splitting four interleaved routing-kind issues into separate commits while the work was actually done in parallel needed pragmatic compromise. The infrastructure landed under whichever issue introduced the most schema/canvas/inspector machinery (240, since it added the multi-kind dropdown + n_outputs control + set_n_outputs extension all in one logical step). The other three issues' commits stay thin because their per-issue work is genuinely small — just a fixture, a test entry, and the closeout. "One commit per issue" as a rule scales when the work is per-issue separable; when it isn't, biasing toward "first-numbered issue carries the shared infrastructure" reads honestly in git log because the commit message says so.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

All four routing kinds shipped end-to-end: schema, runtime, editor, fixture, closeout. Phase-2 progress now has rows for 240/241/242/243. Working tree clean of my work, only your pre-existing untracked WIP left (247, 249, readme.md). Done.

## User

Can we make an issue file to make a box that's a timer? All it does is have a "tick-tock rate" that is either defined in the editor or given as an input value. The map shouldn't compile if there's no wires attached to this box AND there's no value defined in the editor. If there's a wire attached but no value has come in yet, it shouldn't run, but every time it runs it emits a single "true" boolean as it's output. When it receives a value, it should add itself to the thread pool queue as any other box, and then when it finishes it re-adds itself. If the timer value is ever set to 0, then when it re-adds itself it instead just stops. It can be restarted by adding another timer value as input, because when input slots are filled they are also added to the task queue as part of the normal operating procedure for any box.

how can we implement this without endlessly spinning with an otherwise empty queue, and without locking a thread in a sleep, and without a single timer thread running in the background?

## Assistant

Wrote `issues/251-timer-box-tick-tock-emitter.md` with the full design + open questions + suggested implementation steps.

Now your tough question directly: **how to wait between ticks without spinning, without locking a worker in sleep, and without a dedicated timer thread.**

My read of the design space — four options, with my pick at the end:

**Option A — extend the pool's idle-wait with a deadline.** The pool's worker threads already block on a condvar when no work is queued. Today that wait is "infinite until signalled by a new task." Change it to "wait until either new work arrives OR the next-scheduled-timer's deadline." A small priority queue inside the pool holds `(deadline, box_idx)` pairs; the idle worker uses `pthread_cond_timedwait` with the head's deadline as its timeout. On wake, drain expired deadlines into the work queue, then proceed normally.

**Option B — `timerfd_create` + `epoll`.** Each timer gets a kernel-managed file descriptor that becomes readable after its deadline. The pool's idle worker calls `epoll_wait`; kernel coalesces N timers into one wait. More machinery, but generalises to network / file boxes later.

**Option C — pure YARQ requeue at scheduler frequency.** The fire always re-queues itself immediately; on re-pull the worker checks if `now >= deadline` and YARQs back to the tail if not. **This violates your no-spinning constraint** — an otherwise-empty queue burns CPU round-robining a single non-ready timer task. Reject.

**Option D — same as A but with the priority queue inside the dispatch layer rather than the pool layer.** Functionally identical to A; the question is just which layer owns it. The pool owns the idle condvar, so the pool feels like the right home.

**My recommendation is A.** It satisfies every constraint cleanly:

- **No spin:** the worker is in a blocking system call (`pthread_cond_timedwait`).
- **No locked-in-sleep worker:** the worker doing the wait is *already* the idle worker the pool has when there's no queued work. You're not adding a new wait, you're tightening the timeout on the existing one. A new task arriving signals the condvar and wakes it just like today.
- **No dedicated timer thread:** whichever worker happens to be idle does it. If 14 workers are busy, none is doing the wait — the timer just fires when the next idle moment arrives, possibly slightly late. That graceful degradation is the right behaviour for a real-time pipeline that's overcommitted.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The subtle bit in your three constraints: **the pool already has an idle worker waiting on a condvar.** That's not "locking a thread in a sleep" in the sense you meant — it's the pool's correct idle behaviour. The trick is that we're not *adding* a wait; we're *parameterising* the wait the pool already does. The cost of the timer feature is zero additional threads, zero additional condvars, just a `+deadline` argument to one existing call site.
- A question back to you: **do you want the timer's first tick to fire at `now + rate_ms` (one-rate-of-wait before the first event) or at `now` (fire immediately on graph load, then tick every rate_ms after)?** Standard cron-style schedulers default to the first; "kick off a chain at startup" use cases want the second. I left it as an open question on the issue with a slight lean toward "fire at `now + rate_ms`" because that's what `setitimer` does, but either is defensible.
- Another question: **when a timer is still pending and the map quiesces around it** (no other tasks queued, all consumers done), does the run terminate or wait for the next tick? The natural answer for a long-running event pipeline is "wait" — the timer prevents quiescence. The natural answer for a test fixture is "terminate" — quiescence ignores pending timers. A `background: true` flag would let the user pick per timer, but adds schema surface. Lean toward "always prevents quiescence; introduce the flag if a test fixture asks for it."
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

176	   binaries whose names start with `009`.
177	
178	Concept: glob `build/tests/<name>-test`, sort by filename (which
179	sorts by the project's leading numeric index), run each in turn,
180	capture stdout/stderr, parse the binary's trailing
181	`N passed, M failed` line for the verdict.

183	Output shape:

185	  009-slot-store-test                          16 / 16  ok
186	  010-graph-loader-test                        13 / 13  ok
187	  015-large-value-heap-test                     8 /  8  ok
188	  ...
189	  113 / 113 tests passed (14 binaries)
190	```
191	
192	A failing binary prints its captured output below the summary
193	line. Exit code is zero iff every binary passes; non-zero with the
194	count of failing binaries otherwise.
195	
196	Convention compliance per CLAUDE.md: hard-coded `${DIR}` at top
197	with arg override, all paths under `${DIR}`, each shell command on
198	its own line, lives at `scripts/run-unit-tests.sh`.

250 rewritten. The shape now:

- **Three intent-named variants** (`decision` / `confidence` / `calibration`) replace the old `shape`-by-mathematician-name + `out_range` split. Each carries its own midpoint, output range, and composition semantics. The user never has to know what tanh is.
- **Bounds-mode is decided by which sides the user pinned.** `min` + `max` both supplied → fixed; neither → auto; one supplied → asymmetric (that side fixed, other auto-tracked). Same presence-is-mode rule applies to `midpoint`.
- **Dampening as EMA toward the midpoint** for auto sides, with a minimum-gap floor; the supplied-midpoint case anchors the EMA target, the no-midpoint case lets the midpoint follow the data.
- **Clamping as "certainty threshold"** — your reframe. Per-variant defaults: confidence / decision clamp; calibration extrapolates (no certainty semantics).
- **Output is always a double**, and the wire carries the *response* (the smoothed [0,1] or [-1,1] number) rather than the scaled input. The user composes `input × response` in a downstream multiplier if they want.
- **Steepness `k`** as a sensible default + inspector knob + reconfigurable via 320. SVG preview with the middle-80% guides stays in scope (cute is justification too).
- **Per-box atomic min/max cells**, not per-worker or per-thread. Auto bounds non-deterministic across runs, by design; no debug output — wire a log box if you want the trajectory.
- **No persistence** across runs; user supplies fixed bounds if they want carry-over.
- **Strict string parsing** (no LLM-output number extraction — your own conclusion); boolean coercion handled per the C-style 1/0 convention with a fixture to lock it.

What's still open in the doc: the kind's name (`nonlinearity` / `squash` / `remap`), the default variant for new boxes, and the calibration variant's out-of-range mode (extrapolate vs hard-error vs clamp-to-1).

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The biggest design move here was your **"presence of a bound IS the mode for that side"** insight. It collapses three separate flags (`mode`, `fixed_min_flag`, `fixed_max_flag`) into a single JSON-shape rule: a field is either in the object or it isn't, and that's the answer. The C side then mirrors with two `is_fixed` booleans next to the two doubles — same information, two representations, both natural for their respective audiences. The schema becomes self-describing: a reader sees what's set and knows what mode the box is in without having to look up a flag's meaning.
- The decision to **emit the response, not the scaled input** is the call that makes this kind composable. If the nonlinearity scaled-and-multiplied internally, every consumer would get back a number whose meaning depended on the bounds the nonlinearity happened to be using. Emitting the response gives every consumer the same `[0, 1]` or `[-1, 1]` scale, regardless of what the nonlinearity is scoring against. Then "I want the scaled input" is a separate, optional composition the user opts into with a multiplier box. Same pattern as the `write` box keeping its `value` input separate from its `path` input — small box, single responsibility, the user wires together the pipeline they want.
- The doc preserves your dump-truck-and-raccoons line at the very bottom under "Notes on architecture." It's not just for flavour: that note is the design philosophy for what to do when a user holds the box wrong, and it belongs in the doc that someone reads when they're about to make exactly that choice for their own future kinds.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

The rewrite is unstaged. Want me to commit it, or hold while you take another read?

What landed:
- **Schema** (`src/001-schema.lua`) — `nonlinearity` kind, three valid `shape` values, type-checks the optional `min` / `max` / `midpoint` / `k`.
- **C loader** (`src/010-graph-loader.h` + `.c`) — `ROUTING_NONLINEARITY` enum, `nonlinearity_shape_t`, eight new fields on `routing_t` including the per-bound `is_fixed` booleans and the two atomic running cells (uint64 bit-cast doubles), parser with sentinel-init (`+inf` / `-inf` for the running min / max so the first widen always succeeds).
- **C dispatch** (`src/012-dispatch.c`) — `ROUTING_NONLINEARITY` case in `push_routed`. Reads the input value, coerces booleans, CAS-loops widen on auto sides, computes the curve per variant, clamps under fixed mode for confidence / decision, extrapolates for calibration, EMA-dampens the auto bounds toward the midpoint each fire, emits the score as `%g`-formatted bytes on the single output port.
- **Editor** (`assets/js/004-inspector.js`) — `nonlinearity` dropdown option, default routing (`shape: 'confidence'`, `k: 1`), per-kind controls (variant dropdown with hover tooltips per variant; three bound inputs that show blank = auto-track; steepness input; footer note that the wire carries the score not the input), `set_nl_field` setter that applies the presence-is-mode rule (empty bound input deletes the field; number sets it).
- **Build** — `Makefile` gains `-lm` for the new `tanh` / `exp` calls.
- **Three fixtures** — one per variant, each pinning the input to a deterministic point of the curve and asserting the exact `%g` output: confidence at midpoint → `0.5`, decision at midpoint → `0`, calibration at 25% → `0.25`.

Suite 31 → 34 passed, no regressions.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The **uint64 bit-cast trick for atomic doubles** is the right move in C11 — `_Atomic double` works on most platforms but isn't strictly required to be lock-free, while `_Atomic uint64_t` is. The union-based bit-cast (`pun.d = score; atomic_store(cell, pun.u)`) gives us lock-free atomic widening without depending on a compiler-specific guarantee.
- The `*3` factor inside the sigmoid (`1 / (1 + exp(-k*t*3))`) is the small tuning constant that makes `k = 1` produce the doc-promised "middle 80% maps to [0.27, 0.73]" behaviour. Without it, raw sigmoid on `t ∈ [-1, 1]` is too gentle — the curve barely bends. The factor centres the action band at `k = 1`, which is what the user wanted as the forgiving default. A future `k` higher than 1 sharpens proportionally; `k = 2` gives the kind of soft AND that's useful for evidence accumulation.
- The **per-bound atomic widen + non-atomic EMA dampening** combo is deliberate. The widen has to be atomic because two concurrent fires could both see an out-of-range value and need to settle on the larger of the two. The dampening is the *opposite* direction (pulling toward the midpoint), so a concurrent race between two fires both writing slightly-decayed values is benign — both are pulling toward the same target, the later store wins, the bound stays well-behaved. Saving the CAS overhead on the common path (every fire dampens; only occasional fires widen) makes the kind cheap to run.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

## Assistant

Pause-with-you mode rather than implement mode. Let me walk through what your proposal actually computes, then surface the question I think is load-bearing.

**Your proposal, distilled:**

- Output range: a toggle between `[0, 1]` and `[-1, 1]` (one design dimension instead of three opaque variants)
- Bounds: ring buffer of the last N observed values; `min = min(buffer)`, `max = max(buffer)`
- Output: linear remap from the data bounds to the scope range
- (No sigmoid, no tanh, no `k`, no drift — all gone)

What you've just described is essentially **automatic gain control with a sliding window** — same shape audio compressors use. It's a *clean* design and significantly simpler than what's currently in the tree. The math is one division per fire and the parameter surface is two knobs: range and buffer size. A math user reads it and immediately knows what it does; a non-math user reads "normalize my values to 0–1 over the last 100 samples" and also immediately knows what it does. Your naming concern goes away because there's no opaque variant — there's only one operation.

**What's lost** if we drop the S-curves entirely: the soft-AND composition property. Two `confidence` values near 0.5 multiplied together stay near 0.25 (uncertainty stays uncertain); two near 1.0 stay near 0.95 (confidence reinforces). That's the "noise rejection in evidence-accumulation pipelines" thing I wrote up. It's a real property of sigmoid, and it's the only thing that distinguishes this kind from "scale a number to a range." If you never plan to compose normalized scores by multiplication into downstream perceptron-like networks, that property is **moot** — and the simpler linear box is strictly better.

**Ring buffer vs EMA decay:** they're roughly equivalent for matching N and α. Ring buffer is more intuitive ("I remember the last 100 values"); EMA is cheaper (two doubles instead of N) and produces smoother bounds. Your "discrete is more honest" preference is aesthetically defensible and I don't think it's the load-bearing call.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The reason you keep circling on this design is that you're trying to pick a shape without knowing the use-case. That's the right instinct to notice. A design that's general enough to fit every imagined use-case usually fits none of them well, because the trade-offs go in different directions for different use-cases.
- "Decision" and "calibration" were my translation attempt — bridging math to intent. But your point about math-background users is sharp: they don't recognize "decision" but would recognize "sigmoid" instantly. A bridge that confuses both directions is worse than picking one audience and naming for them.
- Linear AGC ≠ less powerful. It's *differently* powerful. The S-curve gives you smooth saturation; AGC gives you adaptive scaling. Most "I want a number between 0 and 1" use cases want AGC. The S-curve use cases are specifically about compositional logic with downstream multipliers.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

**The question I want to ask back** before any code changes:

**What's the smallest concrete use-case where you'd actually wire one of these into a map?** If you can sketch one example — "I have a sensor reading that comes in at unpredictable scale and I want a slider to land between 0 and 1" or "I'm building a perceptron-like decision lattice where multiple confidence scores feed an aggregator that picks an action" — the design falls out of it. The first asks for linear AGC; the second asks for sigmoid. *Both* asks for both. No examples in mind asks for the simplest thing that could work.

Three paths I see, ordered most-to-least conservative:

1. **Rip out what's there, replace with linear-only + range toggle + ring-buffer bounds.** Simplest. Drop "nonlinearity" as the kind name — call it `normalize` or `scale` or `auto-range`. The S-curve story becomes a separate routing kind issue if a use-case ever appears, and the math name (`sigmoid` / `tanh`) is the right name for that future kind because its audience is math-aware.
2. **Keep what shipped, add the simpler linear-AGC alongside as its own kind.** Two routing kinds. The user picks by intent: "I want soft logic composition" → nonlinearity; "I want adaptive scaling" → normalize. Doubles the surface but covers both audiences honestly.
3. **Refactor the shipped one into a single curve-dropdown.** `shape` becomes `linear` / `sigmoid` / `tanh` (math names, for math users). `range` becomes a separate toggle. Bounds-tracking gets the ring-buffer treatment. This keeps everything but renames the variants and changes the bounds mechanism.

If you can answer the use-case question I'd guess path 1 or 2; if you can't, I'd lean path 1 just because it's the cheapest mistake to fix later.

Want to give me a use-case sketch, or should I leave this for you to mull and pick up another thread?

## Assistant

Refactor shipped. The commit chain reads honestly: 250 → "first attempt as designed earlier"; 253 → "refined after use-case clarified."

**What changed in 253 vs 250:**

| Dimension | 250 (shipped first) | 253 (now) |
|---|---|---|
| User-facing variants | `decision` / `confidence` / `calibration` | `range`: `signed` or `unit` |
| Bounds tracking | Fixed-pin OR per-bound EMA-decayed atomic cells | Per-box ring buffer of last N values |
| Bounds API | `min` / `max` / `midpoint` fields (presence = mode) | `memory` (positive int) |
| Output | Score alone (in [-1,1] or [0,1]) | `v × score` (gated linear unit) |
| Cold start | Emit variant-neutral value | Emit `v × neutral` (so first fire passes some signal) |
| Out-of-range | Clamp per variant (confidence/decision) or extrapolate (calibration) | Auto-extended; new extreme widens the buffer on the same fire |
| Concurrency | Atomic uint64 bit-cast doubles, CAS-loop widen, plain store EMA | Per-box pthread_mutex on the ring buffer |

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The **gated output** (`v × score`) is the move that makes this composable for decision lattices. When score ∈ [-1, 1] and you multiply N of them through a downstream aggregator, the midpoint-near values multiply toward zero (suppress) and the bound-near values pass through near full amplitude (vote with strength). Without the gating, the user would always need to insert a multiplier box downstream to recover the input — and forget to half the time. Building the multiplication into the box matches the actual use pattern.
- The **ring buffer is more honest than EMA** for "remember the last N observed values" semantics. EMA approximates that with one number that drifts; the buffer literally stores the N. A user who wants to debug "what's the current min/max?" can in principle peek the buffer (a follow-up feature) and see the actual values. With EMA, the bound is a smoothed approximation that doesn't correspond to any specific historical event.
- The 250 → 253 trajectory is a small case study in **why iteration is cheaper than perfection**. The first 250 commit took the design as I understood it at the time; the use-case conversation revealed three substantive shape problems; the 253 commit fixes them. Each piece — schema, loader, dispatch, editor, fixtures — was small enough to refactor in place. If 250 had shipped as a months-long monolith there'd be no room to course-correct; shipping it as a small commit means the second pass is also a small commit.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The runner finding **a longstanding `307-c-spec-test::compile_with_cflags` failure that the integration sweep had never surfaced** is the load-bearing payoff of 252. The integration tests catch end-to-end behaviour; the unit tests catch lower-level surface that integration doesn't necessarily exercise. Without a way to actually *run* the unit suite without paying for a full rebuild, that failure sat in the C spec for who-knows-how-long. The runner makes that gap visible the first time you use it.
- Parsing the trailing `N passed, M failed` line is a **convention** the unit tests already followed without anyone writing it down. The runner formalises that convention as the parse target — which means new test files have to follow it too, or their results get synthesised from exit-code alone (run-one's fallback path). Worth a brief note in `docs/006-test-coverage-map.md` if anyone trips on it.
- Captures landing in `tmp/` (RAM-backed via the project's symlink convention from CLAUDE.md) means the runner can re-print the verbose output for a failing binary without re-running it — useful when a binary is slow or non-deterministic. The cost is zero disk pressure and the captures vanish on reboot, which is the right shape for "this is debug noise, not a record."
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

# SoraMech — Architecture

## The structural shell

SoraMech is a structural shell. The thread pool, the slot store, the
dispatch layer, the allocator — these are the steel and concrete of
an apartment building. They hold the roof up. They do not decorate
the rooms.

Box authors design the rooms. Library authors furnish them. The
shell provides the framing, the load-bearing walls, the structural
guarantees of what can hang where. The shell does not know what
colour the curtains are.

> "We are creating a structural shell, like an apartment building
> that is just steel and concrete at first, and the user can build
> the walls and windows and design the doors and movement paths as
> they please. The library authors are doing the actual decorating,
> with tables and chairs and pictures of the beach. We are
> structural, we keep the roof from caving in. To that end, we must
---
# SoraMech — Roadmap

## Phase 1 — Foundation (complete)

Goal: a map you can edit in the browser and execute from the
terminal.

At the end of phase 1, the user can:
- Open the editor at `http://localhost:7700/`, see a canvas, create
  boxes, set their `ref` / `fn` / `inputs`, wire them together
- Save edits as box files on disk via the HTTP file CRUD server
- Run `luajit src/007-runner-main.lua <map-dir>` to execute the map
- Add a custom language driver and have the runner use it

Issues 101–110, all complete and moved to `issues/completed/`.

Demo: `issues/completed/demos/phase-1/`.

## Phase 2 — Editor & graph model (current)

---
# SoraMech — Language Driver System

## Two systems, one filename

Phase 2 used **driver scripts** — shell wrappers under `drivers/`
that the synchronous runner invoked one process per box call.

Phase 3 uses **language specs** — `.so` libraries under `langs/`
loaded by the C pool runner via `dlopen`, with persistent per-worker
runtimes.

Same idea, different mechanism. Phase 3 replaces phase 2 wholesale
when it lands. This document covers both, since the project lives in
phase 2 today and the phase 3 design is fully specified.

## Phase 2 — Driver scripts (current)

A driver is a shell script. It knows how to invoke a function in one
language. The synchronous runner looks up the file extension, finds
the driver script, and calls it.

300	    if (!dl) {
301	        fprintf(stderr, "c spec: dlopen('%s'): %s\n", path, dlerror());
302	        return NULL;
303	    }
304	    h->entries[h->count].path = strdup(path);
305	    h->entries[h->count].dl   = dl;
306	    h->count++;
307	    return dl;

## Assistant

Found it. The two `.so` files have **different checksums** (so the build IS producing different output), but `dlopen` returns the OFF version anyway. That's glibc's well-known same-path cache — even after `dlclose` drops the ref count to zero, `dlopen` of the same path can return the previously-loaded library rather than reading the replaced file from disk. The test exercises a path-reuse scenario that production doesn't hit (real boxes have unique `.so` paths). Fix: use a distinct path per compile in the test, document the limitation. Removing my debug traces first.

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The 307 failure was a **test bug, not a runtime bug**. The C spec was correctly passing cflags through to gcc, the build was producing genuinely different `.so` files on disk, but `dlopen`'s same-path cache kept returning the previously-loaded mapping. Production code dodges this by deriving `.so` paths from box ids (each box gets a unique path), so the cache never returns wrong content. The test was the only place where two builds raced for one path. Fixing the test rather than the spec was the right call — the spec's behaviour is correct under the assumption production gives it, and changing the spec to defensively re-`dlopen` on every invoke would slow every dispatch for a hazard no real workflow hits.
- The docs rewrite **deleted 5 files totalling ~1500 lines and replaced them with 5 files totalling ~750 lines**. The compression isn't because content was redundant — it's because the old docs were oriented around the project's development timeline (what each phase added, how features evolved). A user reading "Phase 2 used driver scripts; Phase 3 uses language specs" has to mentally compute "so what do *I* use?" The new docs answer that directly. The development-history information lives more honestly in the `issues/phase-*-progress.md` files where someone actually researching how the project got here would look.
- The big risk in this kind of doc rewrite is **losing institutional context** — the "structural shell" / apartment-building framing was a load-bearing way to think about why the runtime is shaped the way it is. I preserved a compressed version of it in the overview rather than throwing it out, because it answers the "why is X someone-else's-problem" questions that any user eventually hits. The full philosophy can live in `notes/vision`, which the ToC still points at.

104	## YARQ — the yield-and-requeue barrier
105	
106	A reconfigure has to be atomic with respect to other workers
107	firing the same box. While one worker is rewriting the record,
108	no other worker may read inconsistent state — half the new
109	`inputs[]` array with the old `routing.kind`, for example.

116	
117	**YARQ** — yield-and-requeue — is the project name for this
118	primitive. Mechanism:
119	
120	- One atomic word on the box record (`box->yarq`, or similar).
121	- **Acquire**: CAS from 0 to 1. On success, the worker owns the
122	  box for the duration of the rewrite. On failure, the worker
123	  re-submits its current task to the **tail** of the pool queue
124	  and returns — no busy-wait, no parking, no priority inversion.
125	  The tail (rather than the head) is the **longest distance from
126	  re-running**: the contended worker doesn't immediately
127	  re-collide with whoever is currently inside the barrier; other
128	  pending work runs first.
129	- **Release**: atomic store of 0.
130	
131	The cost is one extra trip through the scheduler for each
132	contended worker. The benefit is that the synchronization
133	primitive is *cooperative with the scheduler* rather than
134	*adversarial to it* — the scheduler keeps doing what it does
135	best (managing many small units of work fairly), and the barrier
136	just nudges contended workers to circle back later.
137	
138	The YARQ barrier is acquired by **every** path that mutates the
139	box record — not just reconfigure but also `connect` (issue
140	319d's runtime wire attachment, which already does its own
141	copy-and-publish atomic dance on the connections array). Folding
142	those into the same barrier means the two mutation paths can't
143	interleave dangerously when both fire at once.
144	
145	-- workers who are just executing the box function should not claim the yarq.
146	   they don't need it - they're just reading values, not mutating them.

161	    "inputs":  [

163	        { "name": "y", "type": "string", "optional": true }
164	    ],
165	    "connections": [

28	existing maps cover only a small slice of the new surface (no
29	queued inputs, no large iterator counts, no fan-in).
30	
31	This issue covers two things that go together: the format and

33	exercises the phase 3 runtime end-to-end.

35	## Part A — Run output
36	
37	### Decoupling from the editor
38	
39	The editor (phase 2) is being scoped down to a pure map editor — it
40	does not know how to run maps and does not display run results.
41	`last-run.json` is therefore not a UI feed. It exists for:
42	
43	- LLM consumption — agents reading the file to understand what a
44	  run did
45	- CLI-driven inspection — a future viewer utility (out of scope
46	  here) that pretty-prints the file
47	- Test harness consumption — the integration tests below diff the
48	  written file against expected output
49	
50	Decoupling means the writer's design is driven by these consumers,
51	not by editor rendering needs.
52	
53	### File format: JSON Lines
54	
55	The phase 2 single-document format does not work when the runner is
56	streaming events from many threads. Use JSON Lines instead — one
57	JSON object per line, each line is one event, the file grows
58	monotonically as the run proceeds.
59	
60	Event types:
61	
62	```jsonl
63	{"event":"run_start", "ts":1234567890.123, "map":"maps/classify-demo", "n_workers":16}
64	{"event":"task_submit", "ts":..., "task_id":42, "box_id":"classify", "worker_idx":-1}
65	{"event":"task_start", "ts":..., "task_id":42, "worker_idx":3}
66	{"event":"task_end", "ts":..., "task_id":42, "worker_idx":3, "duration_us":127, "output_size":12}
67	{"event":"slot_alloc", "ts":..., "slot_id":5, "size":256, "n_cells":1}
68	{"event":"slot_free", "ts":..., "slot_id":5}
69	{"event":"run_end", "ts":..., "duration_us":1850, "n_tasks":7}
70	```
71	
72	JSONL is append-only, which makes thread-safe writing tractable: a
73	single mutex around the write call serializes the lines, and each
74	line is self-contained so a partial line on crash is recoverable
75	(reader skips the broken trailing line).
76	
77	The reader (LLM, viewer, test harness) parses one line at a time;
78	total file size doesn't have to fit in memory.
79	
80	### What gets logged
81	
82	Per-task: submission, start, end, duration, output size. Inputs
83	and outputs are NOT logged by default — for iterator boxes
84	producing thousands of invocations, logging every value bloats
85	the file unbounded. There is a verbosity switch:
86	
87	- `SORAMECH_LOG_VALUES=1` — log inputs and outputs (truncated past
88	  some byte limit, e.g. 4 KB) per task. For debugging.
89	- Default: log task lifecycle but not values.
90	
91	Slot allocator events (alloc, free, coalesce, grow) at a separate
92	verbosity level. Off by default; on under `SORAMECH_LOG_SLOTS=1`.
93	For diagnosing memory issues.
94	
95	### Writer mechanism
96	
97	A single dedicated writer thread inside the runner consumes events
98	from a multi-producer single-consumer ring buffer. Worker threads
99	push event records (small fixed-size structs) into the ring; the
100	writer pulls them, serializes to JSON, and writes lines to the
101	file. This avoids per-event mutex contention — the ring buffer is
102	the only shared state, and a well-written MPSC ring is lock-free
103	on the producer side.
104	
105	Alternative considered: each worker writes its own log file, merge
106	at end. Simpler concurrency, but readers would have to merge by
107	timestamp — and any cross-event reasoning (was task A still
108	running when task B ended?) requires the merge anyway.
109	
110	The writer thread is started after the pool is created and joined
111	before `pool_destroy`. It also handles `run_end` as the very last
112	event, including the final summary.
113	
114	### File location
115	
116	`<map-dir>/last-run.jsonl` (note: `.jsonl` not `.json` — the
117	extension reflects the format change). Overwritten on every run.
118	
119	A rotated archive (`last-run.jsonl.1`, `.2`, …) is out of scope.
120	Users who want history copy the file before re-running.
121	
122	## Part B — Integration tests
123	
124	### Scope
125	
126	End-to-end tests of the pool runner against real map directories.
127	Each test is:
128	
129	1. A map directory under `tests/maps/<name>/`
130	2. An expected `last-run.jsonl` (or a comparison spec) under
131	   `tests/expected/<name>.jsonl`
132	3. A test driver script that runs the map and diffs
133	
134	The test driver is `scripts/run-tests.sh`. It iterates
135	`tests/maps/`, runs each, diffs against expected (with a normalizer
136	that drops timestamps, durations, worker indices — anything non-
137	deterministic), and reports pass/fail.
138	
139	### Test maps
140	
141	Coverage targets:
142	
143	| Test map                  | What it exercises                                    |
144	|---------------------------|------------------------------------------------------|
145	| `hello`                   | Single Lua box, one input, one output                |
146	| `data-only`               | Data box → call box. No inputs, just stored values   |
147	| `fan-out-3`               | One output → three consumer boxes (peek, refcount)   |

149	| `comparator-routing`      | Comparator with all three branches (lt/eq/gt)        |

156	
157	The `*-fail` tests verify error behavior — the runner is expected
158	to exit nonzero with a precise error message. The driver matches
159	exit code and stderr against expected.

163	```bash
164	# scripts/run-tests.sh
165	for test_dir in tests/maps/*/; do

169	    actual=$( "${SOURCE_DIR}/soramech-pool" "${test_dir}" )

175	    else

177	        check_success "${name}" "${test_dir}/last-run.jsonl" "${expected}"
178	    fi
179	done
180	```

1	# 009-slot-store.c — public surface
2	
3	Per-input-port slot store. Allocated once at graph load; each box
4	input port owns one slot, freed when the run ends. The dispatch
5	layer reads and writes through this API; language specs never see
6	slot IDs (issue 303 keeps that boundary clean).
7	
8	## Lifecycle
9	
10	- `slot_store_t *slot_store_create(void)` — empty store; NULL on OOM.
11	- `void slot_store_destroy(slot_store_t *s)` — frees every slot.
12	
13	## Allocation
14	
15	- `slot_id_t slot_alloc(store, cell_capacity, n_cells, flags)`
16	  - Returns `SLOT_INVALID` on bad args / OOM.
17	  - Flags: `SLOT_FLAG_NONE`, `SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED`, `SLOT_FLAG_ATOMIC_COUNTER`.
18	  - `cell_capacity` and `n_cells` are ignored for atomic-counter slots.
19	
20	## Ring-buffer ops (push / peek / pop / has_value / fill_count)
21	
22	- `int slot_push(store, id, data, size, tag)` — 0 on success, -1 on
23	  full / wrong type / size too big.
24	- `int32_t slot_peek(store, id, buf, buf_size)` — returns the cell's
25	  filled_size on success; -1 on empty / wrong type / buf too small.
26	  Does not advance head. Used for 1-cell peek slots.
27	- `int32_t slot_pop(store, id, buf, buf_size)` — drains. Untagged
28	  pops head FIFO; tagged pops the lowest-tag filled cell.
29	- `int slot_has_value(store, id)` — 1 if a value is available.
30	- `int32_t slot_fill_count(store, id)` — number of filled cells.
31	
32	## Atomic-counter slot
33	
34	- `uint32_t slot_read_inc(store, id, mod)` — fetch-and-add. Returns
35	  the pre-increment counter value mod the supplied bound.
36	  `UINT32_MAX` on wrong type or `mod == 0`.
37	
38	## Thread safety
39	
40	- The atomic-counter slot uses `atomic_fetch_add_explicit`; no lock.
41	- Ring-buffer slots use a per-slot `atomic_flag` spinlock around
42	  header + cell mutations.
43	- The store itself is single-threaded for allocation (graph-load
44	  phase); after that, the slot array is read-only and per-slot
45	  operations run concurrently.
46	
47	## Variable-size payloads
48	
49	Slots allocated with `SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE` store payload bytes in
50	the unified allocator (016) and keep only an opaque chunk handle in
51	the cell. Push acquires a chunk (refcount 1, owned by the slot);
52	pop copies the bytes into the caller's buffer and drops the
53	reference, returning the chunk to the allocator's free-lists with
54	an eager neighbor-merge. The reclamation test
55	(`tests/009-slot-store-test.c::large_value_reclamation`) is the
56	regression guard for the previous monotonic-growth path.
57	
58	`slot_store_large_value_bytes_in_use` exposes the allocator's
59	"in use" total for the regression test and for future telemetry.
60	
61	## What's NOT here (deferred)
62	
63	- Size-class free lists for the fixed-size cell arrays themselves —
64	  plain `malloc` per slot for now. Allocator-driven cell allocation
65	  is the next step in issue 302.
66	- Producer-declared output sizes are not yet piped through to
67	  `ua_create`, so the allocator starts with no pre-warmed classes
68	  and learns them by accretion. The graph loader integration is
69	  the follow-on.
70	
71	## Related
72	
73	- Issue 302 — design.
74	- Issue 304 — the dispatch layer that calls this API.
75	- Issue 301 — the pool whose workers contend on these slots.
76	
```

1	/* src/009-slot-store.h — per-input-port slot store, public API.
2	 *
3	 * What it is, in a sentence: a thread-safe pool of ring-buffer
4	 * slots, allocated at graph load time, used by the phase 3
5	 * dispatch layer to route values between boxes.
6	 *
7	 * Slots belong to input ports, not tasks. Each box has one slot
8	 * per input port; the slot persists for the whole run. A wire is
9	 * a routing declaration — when a producer's task finishes, the
10	 * dispatch layer pushes copies of the output into every
11	 * downstream input slot. Fan-out is N pushes; fan-in is N
12	 * producers pushing into one slot. Designed in issue 302.
13	 *
14	 * Three slot modes, chosen via flags at slot_alloc:
15	 *
16	 *   1-cell peek (n_cells == 1, no flags)
17	 *     — for literals and wires from producers that run exactly
18	 *       once. Push once at startup. Every consumer task peeks
19	 *       without draining; the cell stays filled.
20	 *
21	 *   N-cell pop (n_cells > 1, no flags)
22	 *     — for wires whose producer runs many times (iterators,
23	 *       queued inputs). Push appends to tail; pop drains head
24	 *       FIFO. Consumer task pops one cell per spawn.
25	 *
26	 *   N-cell pop, tagged (SLOT_TAGGED)
27	 *     — same shape as N-cell pop, but pop returns the cell with
28	 *       the lowest tag, not the head. Used downstream of parallel
29	 *       iterators where push order is non-deterministic but
30	 *       consumption order must follow the iterator counter.
31	 *
32	 *   atomic counter (SLOT_ATOMIC_COUNTER, n_cells and cell_capacity
33	 *     ignored)
34	 *     — single atomic uint32. Read-and-increment via
35	 *       slot_read_inc(). Used for iterator / randomizer /
36	 *       weighted-routing counters. Concurrent reads each get a
37	 *       distinct value mod the caller-supplied bound.
38	 *
39	 *   large-value (SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE)
40	 *     — for outputs whose size is not known at compile time
41	 *       (multi-MB LLM responses, dynamically-sized arrays). The
42	 *       cell holds only a pointer; the payload bytes live in a
43	 *       large-value heap owned by the slot store. cell_capacity
44	 *       is ignored — push/pop accept any size. May be combined
45	 *       with SLOT_FLAG_TAGGED to get lowest-tag pop semantics
46	 *       over variable-size values.
47	 *
48	 * Synchronization is per-slot. There is no allocator-wide lock on
49	 * the hot read/write path. The atomic-counter slot uses
50	 * atomic_fetch_add; the ring-buffer slots use a per-slot spinlock
51	 * around header mutation (one byte, atomic_flag).
52	 *
53	 * Lifetime is the run. Slots are freed when the store is
54	 * destroyed at the end of the run — there is no per-slot refcount
55	 * and no end-of-stream propagation. Run termination is governed
56	 * by the pool's active-task counter (issue 301).
57	 *
58	 * Errors: a return of -1 from a read/write op means the operation
59	 * could not be performed (empty pop, buffer too small, type
60	 * mismatch). The store does not assert or abort; the dispatch
61	 * layer is expected to check return codes. The hard-crash policy
62	 * applies at the language-spec layer, not here.
63	 *
64	 * What's NOT in this version:
65	 *  - Size-class free lists and coalescing. The design in issue 302
66	 *    describes a segregated allocator with eager-coalesce; this
67	 *    initial implementation uses plain malloc per slot. The pattern
68	 *    is "allocate once at graph load, free at run end", so free-list
69	 *    optimization buys nothing for the current usage. Lands as a
70	 *    follow-on if profiling justifies it.
71	 *
72	 * Variable-size payload support: slots with SLOT_FLAG_LARGE_VALUE
73	 * store payload bytes in the unified allocator (src/016-…) and the
74	 * cell only holds an opaque chunk handle. Push allocates a chunk;
75	 * pop copies the bytes out and drops the chunk's last reference so
76	 * the bytes return to the allocator's free-lists. The store
77	 * lazy-creates its allocator on the first LARGE_VALUE slot_alloc
78	 * and destroys it with the store.
79	 *
80	 * (Issue 302's earlier shape used an append-only arena for this
81	 * path; that arena leaked by design and was retracted on
82	 * 2026-05-19 in favor of the reclamation-capable allocator above.)
83	 */
84	
85	#ifndef SORAMECH_SLOT_STORE_H
86	#define SORAMECH_SLOT_STORE_H
87	
88	#include <stdint.h>
89	
90	#ifdef __cplusplus
91	extern "C" {
92	#endif
93	
94	/* {{{ Types & flags */
95	typedef struct slot_store slot_store_t;
96	typedef int32_t           slot_id_t;
97	
98	/* Forward declaration of the unified allocator handle. Callers that

1	# 012-dispatch.c — public surface
2	
3	Phase 3 dispatch layer. The C function the thread pool runs per
4	task. Currently a skeleton: every spawned task lands in
5	`dispatch_action`, increments the context's `tasks_dispatched`
6	counter, and returns. Real input-reading, spec invocation, and
7	output-pushing land in follow-on iterations.

10	
11	- `void dispatch_spawn(const dispatch_ctx_t *ctx, int box_id, int priority)`

14	  receives `dispatch_task_t *` cast as `void *`.
15	
16	## Types
17	
18	- `dispatch_ctx_t` — graph + slots + registry + pool. Plus a
19	  diagnostic `tasks_dispatched` atomic.

## Assistant

`★ Insight ─────────────────────────────────────`
- The **one-pop-per-cycle invariant** has bigger consequences than just "the issue's mixed-stream example was wrong." It collapses the whole design: a worker can't be mid-gather and discover a reconfigure on a later port, because each cycle visits each port exactly once with no re-entry. That means reconfigure can be applied as a **pre-gather sweep** with no retained values, no name-correspondence rebind, and no two-phase commit on the inputs array. The original design was twenty-step; the audited design is three-step.
- **YARQ is a mutator-side primitive only.** Workers reading the box record don't take it. The clean reading of the user's note is: YARQ protects against two mutators racing each other (reconfigure vs. reconfigure, or reconfigure vs. runtime_connect). Readers get cheap atomic loads. This is exactly the asymmetry that RCU-style structures lean on — many readers, occasional writers, writers serialise themselves but never block readers.
- **Reader consistency is the real design fork.** Today's `connections` array is append-only, so the publish order "pointer first, count second" + reader order "count first, pointer second" guarantees a safe snapshot. Reconfigure breaks append-only — inputs can shrink, rename, reorder. The three options I surfaced (atomic-swap bundle / generation counter retry / readers take YARQ) trade off restructure depth against per-read cost. I've left this open in the issue file because it's exactly the kind of decision that wants user input rather than my guess.
`─────────────────────────────────────────────────`

Audit's now reflected in the issue file. Two design decisions for you before any code lands:

**1. Where to start — 311 or 320?**
311's two leftovers (MPSC ring + JSONL normaliser) are small, self-contained, and would benefit 320 (because 320 adds at least one new event type). 320 is the big one. My recommendation: 311's leftovers first as warm-up + infrastructure, then 320. Tell me if you'd rather flip it.

**2. Reader-consistency shape for 320** — three options I sketched in the issue's new "Reader consistency under mutation — design knob" subsection:

- **A. Atomic-swap bundle struct** — clean, contention-free, restructures box_t. Cleanest snapshot semantics.
- **B. Generation-counter retry** — minimal restructure, small read overhead, retries are rare.
- **C. Workers acquire YARQ on reads** — simplest mechanically, but contradicts your "workers don't claim YARQ" note.

I'd rank these A > B > C. A matches the existing copy-and-publish discipline (just one level up — bundle the whole input shape, not just the connections array), and the per-read cost is one atomic load. Your call?

● **Learn by Doing**

**Context:** This is the foundational design decision for 320 — every other piece of the implementation depends on the reader-consistency shape. A is what I'd pick, but the choice has tradeoffs you might weigh differently (e.g., you might value keeping box_t's current layout flat over the cleanest snapshot semantics; or you might find generation counters more familiar from other systems). Whichever option you pick, the implementation pattern propagates everywhere else: `reconfigure_apply` lives or dies by it, the dispatch's pre-gather sweep code reads it, and runtime_connect's existing copy-and-publish either folds in (A) or stays separate (B / C).

**Your Task:** Reply with which of A / B / C to use, and any rationale you want recorded in the issue file. - **Vyukov MPSC vs. mutex-list, on this codebase:** the mutex queue wasn't a correctness problem — it worked perfectly.
